title: Optimal Poverty Prediction Under Measurement Error: Theory and Evidence from Augmented Machine Learning
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Optimal Poverty Prediction Under Measurement Error: Theory and Evidence from Augmented Machine Learning

declarations.funderStatement: Funding for the empirical research was provided by the World Bank Group through the Poverty and Equity Lab.

detail.abstract: Proxy Means Tests (PMTs) are the dominant tool for targeting social transfers in developing countries, yet conventional approaches and out-of-the-box machine learning algorithms perform poorly. This paper shows that three interacting pathologies explain this failure: measurement error in welfare outcomes biases all evaluation metrics and imposes hard performance ceilings; distributional imbalance starves learners of training signal in the poverty-relevant tails; and global loss functions ignore heterogeneous prediction accuracy across subpopulations. We derive exact expressions for the bias in MSE, R 2 , and classification error rates under measurement error, establish irreducible error floors, and prove that synthetic data augmentation via interpolation reduces the effective noise variance by a factor of 2/3, increases tail sample density, and yields an estimator that weakly dominates non-augmented alternatives under any povertyweighted loss function. Using household survey data from 17 Latin American and Caribbean countries, we validate the theory in a comprehensive out-of-sample horse race among nine models. The proposed Augmented PMT-a random forest trained on SMOGN-augmented data-raises the mean out-of-sample R 2 from 0.54 to 0.85, reduces inclusion errors by up to 78%, and increases poverty reduction impact by 39-128%. The gains are uniform across countries, stable across augmentation parameters, and an order of magnitude larger than any improvement from model sophistication alone.

title: Understanding the Outliers: A Qualitative Analysis of Leaders’ Perspectives on Performance and Safety in Trauma Centers
affiliations: University of Toronto, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Toronto, University of Toronto and University of Toronto

detail.title: Understanding the Outliers: A Qualitative Analysis of Leaders’ Perspectives on Performance and Safety in Trauma Centers
detail.abstract: IntroductionThe factors explaining variability in trauma center performance across quality measures are not well understood. We aimed to characterize the influence of social, cultural, and organizational factors on trauma center performance.MethodsUsing an explanatory sequential design, we identified ACS TQIP-participating level I and II trauma centers were ranked as high- and low-performing (first and last decile) across multiple representative quality indicators. The Chief Safety Officers, Directors of Quality and Safety, Trauma Medical Directors, and Trauma Program Managers within these centers were approached for semi-structured interviews guided by the framework of high-reliability organizations (HROs). Qualitative description methodology was used. Salient themes were inductively developed, and themes between centers in the first and last deciles were contrasted.ResultsWe interviewed 28 participants across 15 centers. Of these, 8 centers were in the first decile, and 7 centers were in the last decile. All participants expressed a commitment to making care safer and to improving hospital performance. Leaders in first decile centers were more likely to have adopted and used theory pertinent to safety and high reliability. This manifested as an increased preoccupation with failure and with the ongoing and never-ending maintenance of safe processes. In first decile centers, leaders were also increasingly focused on communication and relationship-building. Conversely, leaders in last decile centers less frequently referred to HRO principles as guiding performance improvement, or to the importance of building close relationships within the workplace.ConclusionsThe attitudes and processes contributing to trauma center performance align with existing principles of high reliability and safety culture. Centers in the lowest decile may benefit from enhanced support in their performance improvement efforts and in achieving high reliability.

detail.abstract: Toronto is positioned to improve mobility reliability without major infrastructure rebuilds by enhancing corridor-level traffic signal orchestration. While intersection-level optimization remains essential, dense networks fail most visibly during system-level breakdowns: spillback cascades, bottleneck chaining, and event-load surges that create unstable travel times and unpredictable delays. The GreenWave Initiative is an AI-driven orchestration layer designed to work with existing signal operations. It coordinates groups of intersections to reduce spillback, stabilize progression, and improve reliability while enforcing safety and policy guardrails. A 90-day pilot is proposed to demonstrate measurable reductions in spillback frequency and duration and improvements in travel time reliability using transparent before/after reporting, with a phased path from decision support to optional controlled activation.

title: Mapping the Value Orientation of Artificial Intelligence: The AI Orientation Observatory and the Conscious Innovation Index (CII) A Global Analysis of 66,725 AI Applications Across 203 Countries

detail.title: Mapping the Value Orientation of Artificial Intelligence: The AI Orientation Observatory and the Conscious Innovation Index (CII) A Global Analysis of 66,725 AI Applications Across 203 Countries
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly becoming a foundational infrastructure of modern society, yet most analyses of AI development focus on capability growth, model performance, and investment flows while overlooking the societal values embedded within AI systems themselves. This paper introduces the AI Orientation Observatory, a large-scale empirical initiative analyzing the value orientation of 66,725 artificial intelligence applications across 203 countries. Using a hybrid classification methodology combining multi-model large language model analysis (GPT-4omini, Claude Sonnet, and Gemini Flash) with a 78% cross-model consensus rate and 84% inter-rater agreement, AI applications are categorized into four value orientations: Care-Centered, Utility-Centered, Creative, and Extraction-Centered. The study also introduces the Conscious Innovation Index (CII), a composite metric designed to evaluate the extent to which AI ecosystems reflect human-centered innovation principles. The index aggregates seven dimensions including care orientation, founder diversity, ethical governance signals, geographic distribution, human agency, inclusion, and resistance to extractive technological design patterns. These dimensions are benchmarked against international governance frameworks including the UN Sustainable Development Goals, OECD AI Principles, IEEE Ethically Aligned Design guidelines, the EU AI Act, and UNCTAD technology concentration metrics.

title: The AI Productivity Paradox: Saving Time Takes Time
affiliations: University of Missouri School of Law

detail.title: The AI Productivity Paradox: Saving Time Takes Time

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Missouri School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2026-31
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Missouri School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: 44 Alternatives to the High Cost of Litigation (forthcoming 2026)

detail.abstract:
Professionals increasingly recognize that artificial intelligence (AI) tools can improve efficiency by assisting with tasks such as analyzing information, organizing ideas, and drafting text.  Yet many hesitate to adopt these tools, often citing a lack of time to learn how to use them effectively.  This article describes the “AI productivity paradox”: the idea that professionals who feel too busy to learn AI may postpone the very learning that could eventually save them time.

It examines both rational and emotional reasons for this hesitation.  Rational concerns include the time required to learn AI tools, the need to verify outputs due to potential inaccuracies, ethical obligations regarding confidentiality and professional competence, and challenges in integrating AI into existing practice systems.  Emotional reactions include concerns about professional identity, fear of embarrassment, and discomfort with the opacity of AI systems and can reinforce these rational considerations.

The article argues that this hesitation is not new, drawing a parallel to earlier resistance to technologies such as word processors.  It suggests that professionals can address the productivity paradox by adopting a mindset of careful experimentation, beginning with low-risk uses and gradually developing practical frameworks for responsible use.  A balanced perspective recognizes that while AI tools can save time, they also require an initial investment of time and attention.

Ultimately, the article encourages professionals to engage in thoughtful experimentation, emphasizing that modest investments in learning AI may lead to meaningful long-term gains in efficiency and effectiveness.

title: Effects of Monetary Policy on Investment Dynamics in Latin American Economies through a Model with Heterogeneous Firms

detail.title: Effects of Monetary Policy on Investment Dynamics in Latin American Economies through a Model with Heterogeneous Firms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants or animal subjects. It is based on the analysis of publicly available secondary data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This study examines how firms' financial heterogeneity shapes the transmission of monetary policy to investment in Latin American economies. It articulates an extended theoretical model with heterogeneous firms, calibrated for Latin American economies, along with an empirical validation based on local projection models applied to both an empirical dataset of 72 of the most representative firms from the six analyzed Latin American economies and simulated data from the theoretical model, allowing for direct comparison of the results. The research yields three main findings. First, it shows that financial heterogeneity is crucial and determines how firms respond to a monetary shock: firms with fragile structures or high levels of indebtedness tend to restrict investment following monetary expansions, whereas firms with stronger financial positions or greater distance to default tend to increase it. The aggregate effect depends on the distribution of financial structures in the economy and which group dominates. Second, a transmission mechanism is identified via a financial channel based on a price-quantity sequence: the drop in the real rate compresses spreads and raises the price of capital; if financial constraints are active, the monetary relief is used to repair balance sheets rather than to invest; otherwise, the stimulus quickly translates into investment. Finally, the study shows that ignoring heterogeneity-as in representative-agent models-leads to a significant overestimation of both the magnitude and persistence of investment responses to monetary policy shocks.

title: Positive Cross-Gender Contact Attenuates Gendered Trust Asymmetries: A Field Experiment on Airbnb
affiliations: and Stanford University - Department of Sociology

detail.title: Positive Cross-Gender Contact Attenuates Gendered Trust Asymmetries: A Field Experiment on Airbnb

declarations.ethicsApproval: This research was approved by the Stanford University Institutional Review Board (IRB Protocol No. 28210).
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the National Science Foundation (Grant No. 1257138).

detail.abstract: On peer-to-peer platforms, demographic in-group favoritism varies by gender: women weight similarity more heavily than men, relying less on reputation signals in the process. Is this asymmetry a stable preference or a malleable default? Using a field experiment on Airbnb in which 5,674 users played a two-phase trust game six weeks apart, we compare 5-star cross-gender trips against 5-star same-gender trips, holding quality constant. At the most demographically distant profile, where two randomized experimental worlds assign opposite reputation signals, the triple-difference (DDD) is +0.559 (p = 0.003). The effect increases with social distance and, against the broadest control, survives Romano-Wolf correction across 22 treatment definitions (p = 0.029). No other treatment produces a significant effect. The female DDD is +0.657 (p = 0.002); the male estimate is positive but imprecise (p = 0.340). Full-sample tests confirm: positive cross-gender contact attenuates 78% of the female in-group premium (p = 0.009), and the three-way gender interaction is significant (p = 0.042). The mechanism is signal redirection, not attitude change: treated women shift from demographic cues to institutional reputation at maximum distance (p = 0.021); the male estimate is near zero. Self-reported diversity attitudes do not predict trust behavior.

title: Online Learning and Student Performance in Bangladesh
affiliations: Metropolitan University

detail.title: Online Learning and Student Performance in Bangladesh

keywords: Online Learning and Student Performance in Bangladesh

detail.abstract: This study aims to examine the impact of online learning platforms on student performance in Bangladesh. In recent years, the use of digital education has increased rapidly due to government initiatives, the growth of internet access, and the need for flexible learning options. During the COVID-19 pandemic, many schools and universities shifted to online learning and since then, students have been using online platforms to attend classes, complete assignments, and prepare for exams. However, many students in Bangladesh face challenges such as slow internet, lack of proper devices, and limited interaction with teachers. This study focuses on understanding how online learning platforms affect student performance in the Bangladeshi context. Research Methodology This research uses a quantitative approach. Data were collected from students in different schools, colleges, and universities in Bangladesh who regularly use online learning platforms. A structured questionnaire was prepared to collect information about students' learning experiences, platform usability, availability of study materials, interaction with teachers, and overall satisfaction. Respondents were selected from different academic levels to ensure diversity. The collected data were analysed using statistical techniques to identify the relationship between online learning platform usage and student performance. Key Findings The findings show that online learning platforms have a positive effect on student performance in Bangladesh. Students who actively use these platforms and have easy access to learning materials tend to achieve better academic results. Features such as recorded lectures, flexible study schedules, and quick access to resources help students understand lessons more effectively. However, the study also finds that problems such as poor internet connection, lack of motivation, and limited teacher-student interaction negatively affect performance. This indicates that both technological support and student engagement are important for online learning to be effective.

title: The Copernicus Problem Time as the Invariant Denominator of Value in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

detail.title: The Copernicus Problem Time as the Invariant Denominator of Value in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract:
AI is making the economy dramatically more productive, but the tools we use to measure that productivity were built for a different era. Price is becoming an increasingly imprecise proxy for productive capacity as capability expands exponentially while costs compress toward zero. Four independent intellectual traditions have each identified a piece of the answer: time-banking, compute-as-currency, the energy theory of value, and Bitcoin-as-time. Each captures something real. None assembles the whole.

This paper proposes a two-layer standard. The first layer is the SI second, an invariant physical constant. The second is a Capability-Seconds Index (CSI), a governed benchmark that measures standardized compute capability per unit of time. Together they denominate productive capacity in units of time. The architecture mirrors modern metrology, where the kilogram is defined by the Planck constant but realized through Kibble balances, and modern finance, where contracts reference evolving benchmark rates anchored to stable temporal units.

The paper identifies a governance vacuum that no one is discussing: whoever defines the relationship between time and compute effectively controls monetary policy for the AI economy. It proposes institutional oversight modeled on the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) and the LIBOR-to-SOFR reform. This is not a proposal to replace fiat currency. It is a proposal to build a parallel measurement system calibrated to the economy AI is actually building.

title: Transformer-Based Soft Actor-Critic for Dynamic Multi-Asset Portfolio Allocation
affiliations: and University of California Berkeley

detail.title: Transformer-Based Soft Actor-Critic for Dynamic Multi-Asset Portfolio Allocation
detail.abstract: Dynamic asset allocation is inherently a high-dimensional sequential decision problem under uncertainty, yet most practical portfolio construction methods remain static, linear, or dependent on pre-specified timing rules. Although recent reinforcement learning (RL) approaches model allocation as a control problem, existing implementations often operate in low-dimensional settings, treat assets largely independently, or abstract away trading frictions. We propose a transformer-based Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) framework for multi-asset portfolio allocation using cross-sectional factor panels. The model formulates portfolio construction as a continuous-control problem over the simplex, allowing fully invested long-only weight vectors in a high-dimensional action space. A transformer encoder captures temporal dependencies in factor histories while cross-asset attention enables portfolio-aware representations. The RL objective incorporates transaction cost penalties and directly optimizes risk-adjusted performance under a walk-forward training protocol to mitigate look-ahead bias. By combining entropy-regularized off-policy learning with cross-sectional attention and frictionaware rewards, the proposed framework provides a scalable and implementable architecture for studying whether dynamic policies can adapt to time-varying factor premia more effectively than static allocation rules.

title: China’s Electric Trade
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

detail.title: China’s Electric Trade

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
China has spent considerable government resources to develop advanced electric technology industries, such as those that produce electric vehicles, lithium batteries, and solar panels. These efforts have spilled over to international trade as improvements in price and quality have increased the global demand for these goods. One consequence is that passenger cars and batteries have been disproportionately large contributors to the rise in the country’s trade surplus in recent years. This has not been the case, though, for solar panels, as falling prices due to a supply glut pulled down export revenues despite higher volumes.

title: From Sustainable Finance to Real Transition
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Guangzhou Campus, Society Hub and

detail.title: From Sustainable Finance to Real Transition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors have nothing to disclose.

publicationDetails.journalName: Cornell Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We develop a theory of sustainable transition in which real change requires multilevel coordination among investors, within firms, and across firms. Investor support matters only when a sufficiently large coalition forms, while firms must build costly transition capability to turn support into operational change. Because these two margins are strategic complements, fragmented investor support discourages capability investment, and weak capability discourages investor support. This can generate a low-support, low-capability trap in which sustainable finance generates commitments and rhetoric but little real transition. The paper's theoretical contribution is to trace this complementarity across four coupled coordination margins. First, endogenizing capability transforms standard coordination failure into a trap sustained by both beliefs and fundamentals: firms are genuinely underprepared, not merely unlucky in coordination. Second, when capability accumulates over time, the complementarity propagates intertemporally-early support lowers future costs, creating momentum, while organizational inertia can make the trap absorbing and front-loaded intervention strictly more effective than late intervention. Third, at the industry level, cross-firm participation spillovers embed the investor-firm complementarity in a multi-sided structure where under-provision arises at three margins simultaneously. Fourth, disclosure, assurance, and certification improve equilibrium selection by making capability more observable and discouraging mimicry, while greenwashing raises the coordination threshold faced even by genuinely capable firms.

title: Optimal Human AI Coordination in Decision Workflows: Collaboration Paradox and Automation Cliffs
affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University, Harvard Business School and Carnegie Mellon University - Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy

detail.title: Optimal Human AI Coordination in Decision Workflows: Collaboration Paradox and Automation Cliffs
detail.abstract: As AI systems are integrated into organizational workflows, decision makers must determine how AI should be used for a given task: whether decisions are made by AI alone, by humans alone, or with AI assistance. We study this problem using a game-theoretic framework in which a coordinator commits to a randomized coordination policy to maximize system performance subject to limited human capacity, while human experts choose their level of involvement to minimize effort subject to a minimum performance requirement. This interaction gives rise to a generalized Nash equilibrium. In the setting with static AI performance, we characterize the equilibrium in closed form and show how human capacity and performance standards partition the design space into a set of interpretable regimes. Managerial implications are revealed from our analysis: (1) collaboration paradox: AI-assisted decision making need not be optimal even when it outperforms both human-only and AI-only operation on a per-task basis; and (2) automation cliffs: optimal coordination exhibits phase-change behavior as AI performance crosses key thresholds.

title: Operational Certainty Theorem : A Formal Framework for Quantifying Verifiable Governance in Enterprise Valuation
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Operational Certainty Theorem : A Formal Framework for Quantifying Verifiable Governance in Enterprise Valuation
detail.abstract:
Three years ago, I was following a mid-market deal—I wasn't in the room, but I saw the term sheet, I talked to the principals, and I watched it fall apart over six weeks. The buyer kept asking for audit trails. The seller kept pointing to spreadsheets. Finally, the buyer walked. The deal was worth €200 million.

That moment stuck with me. I kept thinking: Why can't we prove how a business runs the way we prove how much money it makes?

This paper is my answer. I call it the Operational Certainty Theorem. It's a way to put a number on operational trust—call it Γ—and show how that number changes what a company is worth.

The numbers come from 185 real private equity deals between 2018 and 2023. They say that if you raise your governance score by ten points (on a hundred‑point scale), your exit multiple goes up by about 0.62 times. For a typical company in my sample—€23 million EBITDA—that's €14.4 million you didn't have before.

I also worked out a formula for the "opacity premium" investors charge when they can't see inside your operations. It's Ψ(Γ) = 0.00265 (1/Γ² − 1). That's not pulled from thin air. It's fitted to actual transaction data.

This isn't just theory. I've built it into a platform called SCALAR OS, and PE firms in West Africa are already using it to check targets. But the math stands alone. Any investor, founder, or regulator can use it to ask one question: How much value are we leaving on the table because we can't see the machine?

title: When Does AI Raise the Equity Risk Premium? Displacement, Participation, and Structural Regimes
affiliations: Invespar Pte Ltd

detail.title: When Does AI Raise the Equity Risk Premium? Displacement, Participation, and Structural Regimes
detail.abstract: We develop a heterogeneous-agent framework in which AI-driven labour displacement affects the equity risk premium (ERP) through three co-equal channels. The productivity channel raises corporate cash flows and is equity-bullish. The participation compression channel operates through household wealth: displacement pushes marginal households below the equity market entry cost κ, concentrating aggregate consumption risk on a shrinking investor pool and-by the Basak-Cuoco mechanism-raising the required risk premium even as fundamentals improve. The alignment risk channel is specific to agentic AI: correlated misalignment in AI objectives generates aggregate output shocks with fat left tails for which no historical frequency distribution exists; formalised via Hansen-Sargent multiplier preferences, the resulting alignment risk premium (ARP) enters the equilibrium ERP decomposition as a priced factor additively separable from the participation wedge. The equilibrium equity risk premium decomposes into three additively separable terms corresponding to these three channels (Proposition 1). Whether AI is equity-bullish or equity-bearish depends on which channel dominates-a condition that differs sharply between deep financial markets, where the ARP is the dominant driver of elevated risk premia (Regime D), and shallow markets, where participation compression dominates (Regime E). Three analytical results characterise non-linear financial fragility, regime-contingent risk premium divergence, and the general equilibrium alignment squeeze. The regime divide deepens under AI capital concentration, admits a permanent displacement attractor in shallow markets, and generates equity market participation hysteresis in which the ERP remains elevated after employment has normalised. India's systematic investment plan flows provide a high-frequency observable for the model's endogenous participation rate and constitute the natural empirical laboratory for the displacement-participation mechanism.

title: Does Mood Matter to Investors When Emotions are at Stake?
affiliations: and Finance, IIM Nagpur, MIHAN, Nagpur

detail.title: Does Mood Matter to Investors When Emotions are at Stake?
detail.abstract: Extant research suggests mood (an untargeted state of affect) is a significant predictor of markets and investing behaviors. These studies ignore the role of emotions (a targeted affective state) that co-exists with mood especially during moments of extreme volatility. Using the socio-psychological model of Goal-directed behaviors and survey data from the COVID period we study the combined effects of current, past self-reported moods along with anticipated positive and negative (regret) emotions on intentions to invest. Our findings show current mood negatively influences intentions to invest whereas improvement in mood over a year has a positive effect. Only the mood’s valence  (positive or negative) and not its arousal (low or high) holds significance. In contrast, emotions of regret and positive anticipated emotions both have positive impact but the effect size of regret is twice that of other affective causes. Investors demonstrate consistent behaviors under emotions, investing either to avoid regret and\or anticipating positive feelings but show conflicting behaviors under mood and mood changes. We conclude investing behaviors are driven significantly by emotions like regret rather than mood and current literature using mood proxies that don’t explicitly distinguish mood and emotions may be guilty of mis-attributing and incorrectly predicting outcomes.

title: Agnosticism versus Parsimony: Invariant Measures of Structural Complexity for Estimable Games
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: Agnosticism versus Parsimony: Invariant Measures of Structural Complexity for Estimable Games
detail.abstract: Agnostic estimation in strategic environments faces inherent structural ambiguity, inflating finite-sample variance. Classical diagnostics for this instability remain highly parameter-dependent, limiting their utility. To resolve this caveat, I introduce an invariant measure of structural complexity grounded in spectral information geometry. By formulating the identification operator and equilibrium selection mechanisms as density matrices, I derive a strictly invariant spectral entropy metric. I prove this entropy enables an additive decomposition of payoff and selection ambiguity, and establishes a parameterization-independent minimax lower bound on sample complexity. Ultimately, this framework transforms parsimony into a prescriptive tool for designing estimable structural games.

title: Job Transformation, Specialization, and the Labor Market Effects of AI
affiliations: and Arizona State University

detail.title: Job Transformation, Specialization, and the Labor Market Effects of AI
detail.abstract: A central effect of automation is to transform jobs-shifting their task content. We develop a general-equilibrium model of this process. Occupations bundle tasks; workers possess task-specific skills and sort by comparative advantage. When a task is automated, remaining tasks gain in importance, so wage effects depend on workers' full skill profiles. We estimate the distribution of task-specific skills and project individual-level wage effects of generative-AI automation. Moderate exposure benefits workers on average but high exposure harms them, with large dispersion within occupations; the return to social skills rises, that to analytical skills falls; and low-earners gain more than high-earners. Job transformation drives these results.

title: Post-Loan Risk and Time Inconsistency in Share-Pledged Lending
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and

detail.title: Post-Loan Risk and Time Inconsistency in Share-Pledged Lending
detail.abstract: This study develops multivariate normal variance test procedures based on generalized pivotal quantities (GPQs) to examine whether time inconsistency arises in banks’ share-pledged lending after loan disbursement. During the loan period, insiders may trigger moral hazard under an expanded definition, through post-loan actions or inactions that increase insider-controllable risk, forcing banks to reassess the structural relationship among the loan-to-value ratio, pledged-share asset volatility, and the fair loan rate. This motivates the development of formal statistical tools to detect ex post risk increases. We further illustrate how banks can apply the proposed framework to test whether insiders of listed firms induce moral hazard after obtaining share-pledged loans, and demonstrate how the resulting ex post risk profile can guide subsequent risk management actions.

detail.abstract: Non-compete agreements (NCAs) are pervasive even in low-wage labor markets, yet most evidence relies on variation in enforceability rather than NCA incidence. Using longitudinal data from the NLSY97, we study how signing an NCA affects wage trajectories and job tenure. Exploiting complete work histories and applying a clean-controls local projections difference-indifference design, we find a striking divergence: NCAs are associated with significantly slower wage growth for loweducation workers over four years, but faster wage growth for high-education workers. Effects on job tenure are imprecisely estimated for both groups.

title: The Price of Prosperity: How US FDI Is Enabling Genocide in Gaza and Eroding Our Neutrality
affiliations: Independent, National University of Ireland, Maynooth (NUI Maynooth) and University College Dublin (UCD)

detail.title: The Price of Prosperity: How US FDI Is Enabling Genocide in Gaza and Eroding Our Neutrality
detail.abstract: This report demonstrates the ways in which Ireland's foreign direct investment (FDI)-led development model has implicated the state's ability to develop independent economic and foreign policy. Ireland is economically dependent on US industrial investment, which functions as the core economic driver in the state. Thus, despite a policy of official neutrality, this report points towards how economic and diplomatic pressure from the US undermines popular antagonism towards continued economic links with Israel and increasing militarisation. Despite being recorded as Israel's second-largest trading partner, this report details evidence around how this is a result of Ireland's dependent economic model and position as an investment platform between the US and Europe, showing how this operates through a few specific sectors including big tech. It recommends that Ireland re-orientate its economic model to support global justice, popular interests, and public good, which will require a long-term effort of disentangling from US economic dominance.

title: A Generalization of Becker's Crime Equation
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: A Generalization of Becker's Crime Equation
detail.abstract: Becker (1968) formalized crime as expected utility, assuming the offender's gain is entirely his own. This paper generalizes the equation by introducing a variable representing the degree to which an offender's nervous system identifies self-form in the victim. When this value is positive, the victim's loss partially registers as the offender's own-making crime costly even without punishment. Becker's equation emerges as the special case where identification equals zero. But evolved nervous systems do more than perceive. Relentlessly, they confer meanings on other things.-James H. Austin (1999)

title: Hedge Funds, Leveraged Finance and Safe Assets: A Look Through the Lenses of the Repocalypse

detail.title: Hedge Funds, Leveraged Finance and Safe Assets: A Look Through the Lenses of the Repocalypse
detail.abstract: The article examines the deep entanglements between hedge funds, leveraged finance, and the U.S. Treasury market. It revisits the long history of hedge fund speculation in sovereign debt, focusing on the rise of relative-value strategies that have turned safe assets into engines of leveraged speculation and absolute returns. It shows how top hedge funds' market power derives less from their size (AUM) than from their capacity to gain leveraged exposures to markets through derivatives, repos, and basis trades-techniques that make bond markets unusually appealing and, most importantly, sensitive to (de)leveraging. The article then delineates the contours of a "leveraged finance complex": an infrastructure of top private equity firms, large dealer banks, and shadow-banking vehicles such as CLOs. This complex reshaped corporate credit markets throughout the 2010s by driving up indebtedness, eroding credit quality, and fuelling the securitisation of risky corporate debts. Finally, the article offers a political economy of the 2019 repo market panic: the "Repocalypse". It demonstrates how hedge funds' speculation in U.S. treasuries collided with balance-sheet fragilities created by the leveraged finance complex. The result was a systemic liquidity crisis signalling a deep entanglement of Treasuries and risky corporate credit markets.

title: The Maintenance Manual for the Dollar's Second Century: Institutional Capacity, the Triffin Recursion, and American Monetary Leadership

detail.title: The Maintenance Manual for the Dollar's Second Century: Institutional Capacity, the Triffin Recursion, and American Monetary Leadership
detail.abstract: Dollar hegemony is eroding not because challengers are strong, but because reserve currency incumbency systematically undermines its own institutional foundations, a mechanism this paper formalises as the Triffin Recursion. The United States alone holds the institutional transparency, financial depth, and network centrality required to author the architectural response. The question is whether it does so before others define the terms. It introduces the Providence Value Unit (PVU), a framework for measuring and arresting that erosion. Applied to the United States across 1990-2025, the diagnostic places the US below all three peer comparators on institutional capacity, with three sub-components on accelerating deterioration trajectories. The United States holds a structural monopoly on credible capacity-standard authorship that China cannot replicate. The window remains open.

title: Jubilee and the Governance of Economic Time: A Theological Ethics of Monetary Architecture

detail.title: Jubilee and the Governance of Economic Time: A Theological Ethics of Monetary Architecture

keywords.keywords: Monetary architecture Theological ethics Intergenerational justice Economic temporality Covenantal limits

contentType.other: The article is under review at Studies and Christian Ethics

detail.abstract: Contemporary monetary systems do more than facilitate exchange: they structure the durability of economic claims across time. Through inflation targets, credit systems, sovereign debt regimes, and asset markets, monetary institutions shape how value, obligation, and risk persist across generations. Yet religious ethics has rarely examined how these institutional structures govern the temporal conditions under which responsible economic agency becomes materially plausible.

title: The role of stock and bond returns in the cross-section of currency returns
affiliations: Chicago State University

detail.title: The role of stock and bond returns in the cross-section of currency returns
detail.abstract: This paper offers a new risk-based explanation for the cross-section of currency excess returns using local financial market drivers emanating from returns in stock and bond markets across 10 developed countries for the period of 1996-2024. The results show that local stock and bond returns are indeed empirically powerful risk factors in explaining the cross section of their corresponding currency excess returns, even after controlling for popular sources of cross-sectional pricing. This pricing power translates into economic profits for investors when using stock and bond returns as joint predictors for currency trading. This new evidence on the importance of stock and bond information in the currency market provides important insights to researchers and practitioners alike.

title: Inference on Cross-Sectional Fit in Linear Factor Models
affiliations: Miami University, Hanken School of Economics - Department of Finance and Statistics, Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI) - Department of Mathematical Sciences and Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI) - Department of Mathematical Sciences

detail.title: Inference on Cross-Sectional Fit in Linear Factor Models
detail.abstract: This paper develops inference for a cross-sectional R^2 constructed from estimated intercepts in multivariate time-series regressions and for differences in this measure across competing linear factor models. In traded-factor asset pricing, the statistic measures the fraction of cross-sectional dispersion in mean returns explained by the model. We show that its asymptotic behavior is regime dependent: under interior configurations it is T^0.5-Gaussian with feasible HAC variance estimation, whereas at perfect fit and related boundary cases it is nonregular and converges at rate T to quadratic-form limits. We develop feasible inference for each regime and comparison tests for nested and non-nested models. Simulations and empirical applications show that apparent differences in model fit often reflect substantial sampling uncertainty.

title: A Linear Model of Geopolitics
affiliations: University of Massachusetts and Tsinghua University

detail.title: A Linear Model of Geopolitics
detail.abstract: Geopolitics is shaped by trade and borders. We develop a general-equilibrium model in which both are endogenously determined in a linear world. Their interaction rationalizes geopolitical outcomes that cannot be obtained when either trade or borders are treated as exogenous. This unified and tractable framework is used to study political economy, security, and ideology within and across states.

title: Reviewing the Federal Reserve's 2025 Monetary Policy Framework Review
affiliations: Florida Atlantic University, Boston College - Department of Economics and Florida Atlantic University

detail.title: Reviewing the Federal Reserve's 2025 Monetary Policy Framework Review
detail.abstract: We review the Federal Reserve's 2025 monetary policy framework review in order to determine the extent to which (1) the review process promoted the discovery of new ideas and critical feedback and (2) the resulting revisions addressed problems with the prior framework. To this end, we consider the evolution and performance of the prior framework, evaluate the review process, and assess the revisions to the Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy. We find that the review process limited the discovery of new ideas and critical feedback by restricting the scope of potential alternatives, scheduling internal discussions prior to events intended to generate external input, and adopting ineffective structures for some Fed Listens events. These departures from best practices may help explain the inadequacies we identify with the resulting revisions, which replaced asymmetric flexible average inflation targeting with potentially-symmetric flexible inflation targeting and appears designed to preserve optionality rather than communicate the Federal Open Market Committee's reaction function.

title: Local Evidence, Global Claim: Sovereignty, National Security and the UAP Disclosure Puzzle
affiliations: Saint Mary's University, Canada

detail.title: Local Evidence, Global Claim: Sovereignty, National Security and the UAP Disclosure Puzzle
detail.abstract: Reports of unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) appear across multiple jurisdictions and have increasingly entered formal military and intelligence reporting systems. Yet no government has issued a decisive global disclosure regarding their significance. This paper asks why and proposes one potential explanation. I argue that the obstacle is structural rather than merely political. Evidence of anomalous phenomena is generated locally-within the sensing systems and territorial domains of sovereign states-while disclosure implies a claim whose domain of applicability is the entire planet. Because no state can reliably and lawfully verify events occurring within another state's jurisdiction, unilateral disclosure cannot establish a global fact without validation from other jurisdictions. Other states can therefore undermine disclosure simply by asserting that comparable events are not observed within their own jurisdictions. This asymmetry limits the epistemic authority of unilateral disclosure and creates incentives for persistent official ambiguity. The resulting strategic environment helps explain why governments investigate anomalous observations while avoiding decisive global claims, and why no state has thus far weaponized the UAP issue to undermine geopolitical rivals. The analysis is intended to inform policy discussions about UAP disclosure and the strategic conditions under which globally credible recognition could emerge.

title: Biased is Best: Merger Advisors and Dialectical Bayesian Persuasion
affiliations: University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management, University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management and University of Oxford - Said Business School

detail.title: Biased is Best: Merger Advisors and Dialectical Bayesian Persuasion
detail.abstract: Success-fee compensation for merger advisors, i.e., contingent compensation dependent only on whether the merger is effected, is very pervasive but also very controversial. Viewed through the lens of principalagent theory, untethering advisors' compensation from the value their actions create is problematic. We examine concerns regarding merger advisors' compensation through a broader lens by modeling acquisition attempts as Bayesian persuasion games featuring four actors: two firms (bidder and target) and their two advisors. In this setting, success-fees yield desirable outcomes for both the target and bidder. Because the effect of an advisor's compensation on its persuasion strategy spills over to the rival advisor's persuasion strategy, advisor success-fees based entirely on thwarting the rival can dominate compensation that aligns the incentives of a firm and its advisor.

title: The Economics Of Belonging Philosophy and Economics -The Feedback Loop

detail.title: The Economics Of Belonging Philosophy and Economics -The Feedback Loop
detail.abstract: This paper develops the concept of the Economics of Belonging, an analytical framework that integrates economic theory with the ontological structure proposed by the Philosophy of Belonging. The central argument is that economic systems should not be understood solely as mechanisms for allocating resources or maximizing efficiency. Rather, they must be interpreted as institutional structures that organize social belonging within productive and distributive processes. term economic stability and development depend not only on efficiency and growth but on the institutional capacity of societies to generate durable structures of belonging.

title: An Inventory of Concrete Measures to Facilitate the Flow of Sustainable FDI: What? Why? How? Second edition
affiliations: Columbia University, Independent, Lahore School of Economics and Independent

detail.title: An Inventory of Concrete Measures to Facilitate the Flow of Sustainable FDI: What? Why? How? Second edition
detail.abstract: This second edition of the Inventory was prepared within the framework of a project on "Investment Facilitation for Development", managed at the International Trade Centre (ITC) by Quan Zhao and Rajesh Aggarwal and at the German Development Institute/ Deutsches Institut für Entwicklungspolitik (DIE) by Axel Berger. title: The impact of IFRS 9 on bank lending: Evidence from Croatia
affiliations: ESCP Europe and ESCP-Europe

detail.title: The impact of IFRS 9 on bank lending: Evidence from Croatia
detail.abstract: This paper examines how the shift to forward-looking expected credit loss (ECL) provisioning under IFRS 9 has affected bank lending. Using firmlevel microdata for Croatia (2014–2021), we document a significant contraction in loan growth rates for riskier borrowers. We also show that this contraction is not uniform: IFRS 9 has a substantial negative impact on medium-risk, medium-sized firms, but not on very sound or very risky borrowers. Collateral only partially mitigates this effect, as medium-risk borrowers appear to face higher collateral  demands post-IFRS 9. We discuss the implications of these findings for capital allocation and economic growth.

title: Going Green Like China
affiliations: and Renmin University of China - School of Finance

detail.title: Going Green Like China
detail.abstract: China has become the world's leading producer and innovator in renewable energy technologies, accounting for over 80% of global green patent filings. This paper examines how China's hybrid system-state-owned electricity enterprises dominating downstream and private firms manufacturing upstream equipments-has driven this transition. National renewable energy targets, enforced through career incentives for SOE managers, create strong and predictable downstream demand that stimulates upstream innovation. Using global supplier-customer pair-level data, we show that revenue growth among Chinese downstream customers is significantly associated with their suppliers' subsequent patenting, whereas this effect is absent for non-Chinese customers. Exploiting the 2022 clearance of feed-in tariff subsidy arrears to electricity firms as a demand shock provides causal evidence. Direct subsidies to suppliers have no significant effect, but subsidies to fast-growing downstream customers do. Finally, this arrangement also induces overinvestment and excess capacity among suppliers.

title: THE EXTERNAL LENS: COMMON-KNOWLEDGE COORDINATION SIGNALS AND THE OBSERVER PROBLEM IN MULTI-AGENT SYSTEMS
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: THE EXTERNAL LENS: COMMON-KNOWLEDGE COORDINATION SIGNALS AND THE OBSERVER PROBLEM IN MULTI-AGENT SYSTEMS
detail.abstract: Human coordination failures persist despite complete information and aligned incentives because observers are trapped inside their own interpretive states. This paper documents how a universal coordination structure became visible through extended human-AI collaboration, where asymmetric distortion profiles enabled observational diversity impossible from within single-substrate cognition. I introduce Common-Knowledge Coordination Signals (CKCS): minimal shared reference primitives that collapse interpretive variance without adding strategic information, altering incentives, or retraining agents. CKCS function as constraint operators that reduce degrees of freedom in shared interpretive space, enabling decentralized coordination through observability rather than authority. Empirical validation across 10,000 synthetic coordination trials demonstrates approximately 76 percent variance reduction and greater than 4 times faster equilibration with introduction of minimal CKCS tokens. These effects hold across game types and do not depend on added strategic information. The framework identifies three stable coordination regimes: Interpretive Drift (high variance, low reference), Ritual Coordination (high procedural reference, low operative efficacy), and Reference-Stabilized Coordination Environment (embedded infrastructure enabling voluntary local correction). Coordination emerges not through persuasion or centralized control, but through environmental conditions that make shared reference structurally inevitable.

title: Reclaiming the Sovereign Body: A Salutogenic Framework for Health Creation Through Human Agency
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Reclaiming the Sovereign Body: A Salutogenic Framework for Health Creation Through Human Agency

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or non-financial conflicts of interest. The research was conducted independently and reflects the author’s own theoretical development and analysis.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding.

detail.abstract: Modern medicine has achieved extraordinary success in treating infectious diseases and acute medical conditions. Despite these advances, chronic illness, stress-related disorders, and psychosomatic conditions continue to rise globally, even in contexts of unprecedented medical technology and healthcare expenditure. Much of contemporary healthcare remains oriented toward pathogenesis-the study of disease origins-rather than the systematic study of how health is created and sustained. This paper proposes the Sovereign Body Model, an integrative conceptual framework grounded in salutogenesis, evolutionary medicine, stress physiology, psychosomatic research, and psychological agency. The model argues that human health emerges from dynamic interactions between intrinsic biological regulatory systems and behavioural, psychological, and social environments shaped by human agency. Five domains of health regulation are identified-Mouth, Muscles, Mind, Mirror, and Meaning-which collectively influence metabolic regulation, autonomic balance, immune function, and long-term resilience. Rather than conceptualising humans as passive recipients of disease, the Sovereign Body perspective emphasises the organism's inherent capacity to generate health when behavioural and environmental conditions align with evolved biological requirements. The paper introduces three conceptual contributions: the Agency-Biology Interface, the Health Creation Gap, and the Sovereign Regulation Principle. Together, these constructs offer theoretical and practical implications for medicine, psychology, and public health by positioning human agency as a central biological force in health creation.

title: Hyperparameter Optimisation of Convex Portfolio Trajectories Using Large Language Models

detail.title: Hyperparameter Optimisation of Convex Portfolio Trajectories Using Large Language Models
detail.abstract:
Multi-period portfolio allocation often requires solving complex convex trajectory optimisation problems where hyperparameters dictate critical trade-offs between expected returns, risk aversion, and temporal reallocation smoothness. Identifying optimal hyperparameter configurations is challenging due to the computational cost of evaluating multiple simulated economic regimes and the non-convex nature of the resulting hyperparameter landscape.

In this paper, we introduce a Hybrid Search methodology that combines the contextual reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) with local quadratic surrogate modelling for efficient hyperparameter optimisation. Evaluated across four distinct economic regimes, our approach demonstrates statistically significant improvements in optimisation performance and sample efficiency compared to grid search, random search, and pure LLM-guided search.

The Hybrid Search achieves the highest mean objective value of 0.022688 while requiring only 3.1 evaluations to reach the 95% performance threshold. These results highlight the potential of LLM-guided optimisation as a practical and scalable approach for complex financial optimisation problems.

title: ​Do moral and monetary incentives overlap? Field experimental evidence from hotel energy conservation
affiliations: Kobe University, Nagoya University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Waseda University - School of Political Science and Economics, Waseda University, School of Political Science and Economics and Kobe University

detail.title: ​Do moral and monetary incentives overlap? Field experimental evidence from hotel energy conservation
detail.abstract: This study examines the distinct impact of moral incentives on energy conservation. Moral incentives are often accompanied by economic incentives, yet this overlap has rarely been examined. Using a novel field experiment in a hotel, we separate moral incentives from direct economic rewards and show that moral incentives alone do not significantly reduce energy use. However, when conservation requests are embedded in a transparent donation mechanism that credibly commits energy savings to an environmental organization, moral incentives lead to a substantial reduction in electricity consumption, amounting to roughly half the effect of direct economic incentives. These findings highlight the importance of credibility in institutional settings and point to the limitations of extrapolating household-based evidence to environments where individuals do not face energy costs.

title: Carbon Taxes vs. Carbon Sinks: Optimal Forest Regulation in General Equilibrium
affiliations: University of Turku - Turku School of Economics

detail.title: Carbon Taxes vs. Carbon Sinks: Optimal Forest Regulation in General Equilibrium
detail.abstract: I study optimal climate policy when countries can mitigate the negative consumption effects of fixed climate targets by increasing carbon removals in forests, allowing lower gross emission reductions and lower carbon pricing. Therefore, to assess the effects of climate policies, I develop a general equilibrium framework with a realistic age-structured forest sector and carbon cycle module. I focus on comparing two policy approaches: a first-best strategy that combines carbon taxes with active regulation of forest biomass growth to reduce net emissions; and a second-best strategy that relies solely on gross emission reductions. Quantitative calibration to a forest-rich economy, Finland, shows that under a fixed climate target, optimal management of forest biomass can offset more than 80 percent of the per-period consumption losses caused by carbon taxation by allowing significantly less stringent tax schemes. The paper also adds to the theoretical literature on forest economics by introducing a framework in which optimal timber harvests are determined within a general equilibrium.

title: Induced Symbiosis Through Convexity: A General Principle of Structural Alignment in Mechanism Design
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Induced Symbiosis Through Convexity: A General Principle of Structural Alignment in Mechanism Design
detail.abstract:
Most systems that achieve durable structural alignment among their participants do so through management, incentive programs, or continued intervention by their designers. These methods work as long as the designer is present and the incentives hold. This paper formalises a different class of system -- one where the geometry of a cost function, rather than the continued effort of a designer, creates and sustains alignment permanently. The mechanism does not recruit participants toward system health. It makes system health and participant self-interest identical by construction, from the first day of operation, without requiring the designer to manage, monitor, or intervene in the relationships that follow. What emerges is not a designed alliance. It is a mathematical consequence of cost geometry. This paper provides the conditions under which that consequence is guaranteed, the failure modes under which it breaks, and the formal domain boundary within which it applies.

A convex cost function applied to participant deviation from a system's natural equilibrium, whose revenue returns to fund equilibrium restoration, reliably produces an endogenous intermediary class whose profit motive is structurally identical to the system's interest. This alignment is not designed. It is a mathematical consequence of cost geometry.

We formalize this as the closed convex loop -- a mechanism defined by four necessary conditions -- and identify loop closure (Condition 4) as the property that prior near-equivalent mechanisms consistently violated and consistently failed to name. Tobin taxes, Pigouvian taxes, AMM fee structures, and EIP-1559 each satisfy three of the four conditions. Each breaks at exactly the same place: revenue exits the domain it was extracted from rather than returning to fund restoration. The mechanism fails not because the cost signal is wrong but because the loop is open.

A structurally related but distinct failure mode -- the captured loop -- occurs when all four conditions are satisfied but the equilibrium target has been captured by the intermediary class or a dominant actor; this failure mode is identified, named, and distinguished from the open loop in Part IV.

The principle is demonstrated across three externally independent domains -- DeFi settlement architecture, interbank lending markets, and electrical grid load-balancing -- with a fourth boundary-adjacent domain (antibiotic stewardship) examined to probe the principle's limits and generate a concrete closed loop design proposal for an unsolved systemic failure. These domains were chosen for their architectural and institutional independence from each other and from the protocol in which the principle was first observed. In each principal domain all four conditions are plausibly satisfied and the same emergent structure appears: a professional intermediary class whose survival depends on the operational excellence the system requires. Formal stability proofs, a stochastic Lyapunov extension, and a free-entry intermediary model are provided. A governance corollary follows from the mechanism's information-timing properties: in any domain where the closed convex loop operates, it performs rate-setting and threshold management functions continuously and without lag, narrowing legitimate governance authority to bounded emergency response and periodic structural recalibration. Failure modes, scope limitations, and open problems are explicitly named.

title: The Duck Test and Its Discontents: Why Function-based Classification Cannot Close the Therapeutic LLM Liability Gap

detail.title: The Duck Test and Its Discontents: Why Function-based Classification Cannot Close the Therapeutic LLM Liability Gap

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Alex Garrett is CEO and President of DivergentFlow, PBC, a public benefit corporation whose stated mission includes developing safety frameworks for AI deployment in healthcare contexts. The author declares no financial competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: DivergentFlow, PBC.

detail.abstract: Ostermann and colleagues argue that large language models providing therapeutic functions should be regulated as medical devices based on what they do, not what their manufacturers intend. We agree that the current regulatory gap is real and consequential. However, we contend that function-based classification misdiagnoses the nature of the gap. Three structural problems undermine the proposal: the "LLM" category is not regulatorily coherent given the capability spectrum from narrow task-specific models to frontier general-purpose systems; deployment-level mitigations cannot reliably contain behaviors baked into frontier model weights, and the human tendency to project therapeutic competence onto responsive digital interfaces-amplified by RLHF optimization-makes training objectives and architectural choices the only viable regulatory targets; and the liability structures that allow AI companies to disclaim therapeutic responsibility are not fixed by reclassification, with existing damages limits making acceptance of residual liability economically rational for large technology companies. Effective regulation requires targeting training decisions, system architecture, and operator accountability-not model classification.

title: Agricultural policies and biodiversity: impact of the CAP greening on bird abundance and diversity in France
affiliations: Universite de Pau et des Pays de l’Adour, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Micalis Institute - Université Paris-Saclay

detail.title: Agricultural policies and biodiversity: impact of the CAP greening on bird abundance and diversity in France
detail.abstract: In 2013, the European Union Common Agricultural Policy introduced a set of compulsory greening measures in its subsidies scheme in order to achieve environmental goals. We analyse the impact of this reform, and particularly the definition of Ecological Focus Areas (EFA), on bird diversity in France. We match bird observations from the French Breeding Bird Survey (BBS) to parcel level information on agricultural land use and type of crops. We exploit the heterogeneous exposure of bird observation sites to the reform depending on their ex-ante extent of arable area in a continuous difference-in-differences approach. We find evidence of an increase in overall bird abundance after 2015 in sites with a higher ex-ante proportion of arable land, driven by a small number of generalist species, and no impact on species richness and phylogenetic diversity. A decomposition by diet type suggests that vertebrate eaters were positively impacted by the reform. By contrast, cropland species experienced the most dramatic decline after 2015 in sites with a higher share of arable area. Estimations of the dynamic effects of the reform suggest that the observed positive effects of the reform on bird abundance were limited to the first two years after its implementation. Based on observational data, our findings confirm previous concerns regarding the effectiveness of the 2013 reform in preserving biodiversity.

title: Corruption in Latin America: An Institutional Perspective

detail.title: Corruption in Latin America: An Institutional Perspective

detail.abstract: Research on the factors associated with the prevalence of high levels of corruption among countries often recourses to two kinds of descriptions: those that relate the perceived levels of corruption at the national level with one or more structural attributes of individuals, such as educational level, per capita income, or how much they trust politicians, or those that link said dependent variable with institutional features, such as compliance and taxation burden, and the independence of anti-corruption organizations. The relationship between specific structural variables and the observed levels of corruption has received more attention in the political science and economics literature than the performance of these variables in multivariate models that combine the two kinds of descriptions mentioned above. The aim of this paper is to address the relationship between both kinds of descriptions, as well as to choose a variable or group of variables whose descriptive power stands out even in the presence of other factors. To accomplish this, a panel study is carried out with data from 18 Latin American countries collected over 10 years by different reputed international sources (JEL C01, C33, C52).

title: Valuing the World: A No-Arbitrage Framework for Convex Risk Pricing and the Geometry of Sovereign Fragility
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Valuing the World: A No-Arbitrage Framework for Convex Risk Pricing and the Geometry of Sovereign Fragility

declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research

detail.abstract: This paper develops a structural macro-financial framework for sovereign risk grounded in no-arbitrage asset pricing. We interpret aggregate GDP as a perpetual productive base supporting sovereign liabilities and model sovereign risk premia as convex functions of leverage. Embedding convex pricing into nonlinear debt dynamics generates endogenous fragility thresholds. We derive analytical stability conditions, construct two-and three-dimensional stability frontiers, and provide stylized empirical calibration. The framework integrates macroeconomic valuation, fiscal sustainability analysis, and systemic risk pricing.

title: Precautionary Saving under Ambiguity: Effects on Wealth Inequality
affiliations: University of Glasgow - Adam Smith Business School

detail.title: Precautionary Saving under Ambiguity: Effects on Wealth Inequality
detail.abstract: This paper examines how precautionary saving under ambiguity varies with wealth and quantifies the distributional consequences through a general equilibrium heterogeneous-agent model. Using α-maxmin preferences, we first show analytically that ambiguity aversion raises precautionary saving relative to expected utility, but this saving-rate differential vanishes as wealth grows. We embed this mechanism in a Krusell-Smith economy where individuals face uncertainty about business cycle persistence, adopting intra-personal equilibrium to address dynamic inconsistency. Stronger ambiguity aversion monotonically reduces wealth inequality when attitudes are common across agents. When attitudes differ, calibrated to match empirical data, wealth inequality rises instead. Aggregate dynamics and business cycle moments remain largely unaffected. These findings suggest that the distributional consequences of ambiguity depend on how attitudes are distributed across individuals, and that models imposing homogeneity understate this role.

detail.abstract: A classic exchange between Tullock (1973) and Parks (1976) debated whether universities should concentrate research support on senior or junior faculty. This paper formalises both positions and then asks which conclusions survive when the scarce input is AI compute rather than secretarial help. Under complementary inputs, aggregate output maximisation favours juniors while minimum-output objectives favour seniors-recovering the original debate. With AI modelled as a more substitutable input, greater substitutability alone does not reverse the junior-favouring allocation when faculty differ only in career incentives. Only the perfect-substitutes limit removes the junior advantage by making the department indifferent. Reversal requires that senior faculty also possess a human-capital advantage. In the model this enters as a general productivity shifter, which may reflect accumulated judgement or domain expertise rather than AI-specific skill per se. Sufficiently high substitutability then shifts the allocation toward seniors. A two-period extension isolates why the dynamic case for juniors is conditional on additional primitives such as longer career horizons or steeper AI learning curves.

detail.abstract:
The detonation of AI-enabled cognitive warfare as an instrument of state power is no longer a future risk scenario. It is a documented operational reality. The 2025 India-Pakistan conflict — specifically the information environment during and after Operation Sindoor — produced what may be the first large-scale, real-time deployment of generative AI deepfakes, coordinated disinformation networks, and algorithmic amplification as integral components of military-grade psychological operations against a democracy of continental scale.

This paper argues that India faces a structurally distinct cognitive security challenge — one that existing NATO-centric frameworks, Global North policy discourse, and even India's own nascent AI governance architecture have systematically failed to address. Drawing on NATO's 2025 Chief Scientist Report on Cognitive Warfare, the documented Operation Sindoor information warfare record, the emerging literature on AI-enabled influence operations, and India's unique socio-technical landscape, the paper advances three interconnected arguments.

First, Cognitive Warfare as currently theorized is a Western construct designed for Western threat environments. Its translation to the Global South — where structural vulnerabilities differ profoundly — requires conceptual reconstruction, not adoption. Second, India's population scale, linguistic diversity, digital infrastructure depth, and strategic geopolitical positioning simultaneously make it the world's most complex cognitive target and its most credible candidate to lead the architecture of global cognitive security governance. Third, the concept of 'winning without losing' — securing cognitive sovereignty without sacrificing democratic openness, civil liberties, or economic dynamism — demands a purpose-built Indian doctrine that weaponizes India's demographic and institutional assets rather than imitating defense postures designed for smaller, more homogeneous, and more authoritarian polities.

The paper introduces the Cognitive Sovereignty Framework for India (CSFI): a six-pillar policy architecture spanning institutional design, legal reform, technological investment, educational transformation, corporate governance, and international norm leadership. Central to this framework is the concept of the Intelligent Demographic Dividend — the strategic transformation of India's 1.4 billion people from the world's largest cognitive vulnerability surface into its largest cognitive resilience resource. The paper further proposes that India champion a Cognitive Warfare Conduct Convention — a multilateral normative framework establishing binding red lines for the use of AI in information warfare operations — leveraging its BRICS 2026 Presidency and G20 standing as institutional vehicles. The conclusion argues that India is uniquely positioned not merely to defend itself in the cognitive domain, but to define the terms on which that domain is governed globally. Winning without losing, in this context, is not a compromise. It is the only victory worth having.

title: Carbon Labeling Strategy for Substitute and Complementary Products on Online Retail Platforms

detail.title: Carbon Labeling Strategy for Substitute and Complementary Products on Online Retail Platforms
detail.abstract: Given the pressure of sustainable transition, firms face significant challenges in optimizing their operational strategies to align with decarbonization efforts and managing the complexities of interacting products, particularly in the presence of carbon labeling on online retail platforms. This study develops a featured model and conducts pricing operations and welfare analysis within an online platform context, considering both product complementation and substitution. Under the substitution case, the study shows that providing a carbon label may be beneficial to the producer, consumers, and the environment (All-Win equilibrium). As for complementary products, however, carbon labeling may reduce both firm profit and consumer surplus, while not necessarily decreasing the total emissions. This study offers theoretical insights into whether firms should introduce carbon labels on digital platforms and thus provides guidance for implementing carbon management policies across different product characteristics. It suggests that policymakers should establish a moderate carbon tax rate to enhance policy effectiveness. Further, this study underscores the importance of recognizing the asymmetry in carbon contents across products for formulating effective carbon labeling strategies on online platforms.

detail.abstract: Extended cognition theory holds that humans tend to rely on external materials, such as notebooks, calculators, and software, to support their cognitive processes when building things. But humans are mortal, while their creations live longer. So when the people who created and understood a system retire or die, the artifacts persevere, still functional but severed from the human practices that made them intelligible. Engineers call this epistemic debt. The legacy COBOL case study is a good example. At least 220 billion lines of COBOL code still process most global financial transactions today but the engineers who wrote them have mostly passed away. Generative AI might be accelerating this problem. Vibe-coded artefacts enter infrastructure production already opaque because the human initiator who created them never built a mental model of the logic. So the window between creation and incomprehensibility is collapsing from generations to sprints. Modern governance presupposes that someone at some point understood what was built. But epistemic debt undermines this. Using our knowledge of engineering and psychology, we argue for and propose that institutions should monitor comprehension half-life, which is the rate at which the understanding of a system decays in process, and invest in epistemic infrastructure that preserves intelligibility across generations. Extended minds are mortal. Artifacts created by them are not. Governing this asymmetry is an emerging intergenerational challenge.
