title: Is it always "the Faster, the Better"? The Role of a Nudging-based Function in the Relationship between Product Delivery and Online Sales
affiliations: Lanzhou University, School of Management, University of Science and Technology of China, University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration and University of Iowa

detail.title: Is it always "the Faster, the Better"? The Role of a Nudging-based Function in the Relationship between Product Delivery and Online Sales
detail.abstract: Delivery time is one of the keys to e-commerce success. Although retailers are taking steps to offer fast delivery services, these approaches are expensive and may not be sustainable in the long term. By leveraging a unique shift resulting from user-interface designs on eBay.com, we find that introducing a nudging-based function, i.e., a guaranteed delivery toggle, is a promising cost-effective approach that may ameliorate the relationship between slow delivery time and product sales. Specifically, our research devises three complementary studies-1) examining the sales impact of the toggle function using a large-scale secondary dataset, 2) investigating the underlying mechanism of the toggle effectiveness through laboratory and online experiments, and 3) analyzing the far-reaching impacts on consumers' subsequent rating behaviors-to establish the external and internal validity and robustness of this finding. We attribute the expansion of slow-delivery item sales (Study 1) to the subtle change in the design of the choice architecture from simultaneous to sequential attribute choices (Study 2). Study 3 reveals the mitigation of dimensional rating bias toward delivery time, further interpreting the nudging effect of sequential attribute choices. Given the dilemma of e-commerce for fast-delivery provision, our research elucidates how practitioners improve their operational decisions to address the last-mile logistics problem by factoring in a simple and free delivery-related nudge.

title: Food Security Dynamics in the United States: A Longitudinal Machine Learning Analysis

detail.title: Food Security Dynamics in the United States: A Longitudinal Machine Learning Analysis
detail.abstract: This study utilizes a longitudinal machine learning framework to analyze the transition probabilities and temporal dynamics of food security in the United States from 1999 to 2023. While 94.16% of secure households maintain their status, those who fall into insecurity become trapped by structural forces that make recovery difficult. Statistical results show that once a household enters a state of food insecurity, the persistence rate is 56.01%, suggesting a high degree of path dependence and limited spontaneous recovery. Further investigation into the drivers of these dynamics shows that transitions are not merely a function of income volatility but are critically tied to structural fixed-cost burdens. Specifically, the model identifies that shocks to housing equity and healthcare insurance expenditures serve as primary catalysts for state transitions. These results suggest that U.S. food insecurity is governed by a high-stability regime for the secure population and a low-mobility trap for the insecure, affecting 19.74% of households through cumulative exposure. This requires policy interventions that target structural barriers to exit rather than temporary income support alone.

title: The Income Hinge: A Structural Statistic for the Transition from Additive Core Dynamics to Multiplicative Tail Scaling

detail.title: The Income Hinge: A Structural Statistic for the Transition from Additive Core Dynamics to Multiplicative Tail Scaling
detail.abstract: This note introduces the hinge income, x h , as a structural statistic marking the transition between additive core dynamics and multiplicative tail scaling in observed income distributions. Building on an earlier note that interprets the exponential core and Pareto upper tail as the outcome of distinct underlying processes, the paper isolates the transition point between these regimes as a distinct object of analysis. The note argues that the hinge is economically meaningful, admits a simple reduced-form characterization, and can be identified approximately using standard empirical threshold procedures. In this way, the hinge captures a structural feature of income distributions that aggregate inequality measures do not directly recover: the location at which additive dynamics begin to give way to multiplicative scaling.

title: Explaining the Global Spread of Collective Litigation: A Law & Economics Perspective

detail.title: Explaining the Global Spread of Collective Litigation: A Law & Economics Perspective
detail.abstract: This paper was developed for the workshop on "The Globalization of Class Actions" (Stanford Law School, April 24, 2026). It explores possible Law & Economics explanations for why representative collective litigation procedures have spread to over fifty jurisdictions in recent decades. The analysis is organized around a simple cost-benefit inequality: a country might adopt such procedures when the expected benefits exceed the expected costs. On the benefit side, the paper considers factors such as the public-goods character of deterrence, the limits of public regulation, regulatory competition, and behavioral herding among policymakers. On the cost side, it examines how technological change, the growth of specialized legal professionals and litigation funders, and the availability of procedural templates may have lowered the barriers to adoption. The paper also touches on how design choices can be understood through this lens.

title: Robots and Public Finances: Evidence from U.S. States
affiliations: Government of the Swiss Confederation - Federal Finance Administration and Ca Foscari University of Venice

detail.title: Robots and Public Finances: Evidence from U.S. States
detail.abstract: How does the rise of industrial robots affect public finances? We address this question by first developing a stylized task-based model in which human labor and robot capital jointly produce output under labor-income and consumption taxation. The model establishes that the fiscal effects of automation are theoretically ambiguous, depending on labor-market adjustments and the structure of the tax system. We then empirically estimate the impact of industrial robot exposure on U.S. state-level public finances over the period 1993-2021. During the early phase of diffusion (1993-2007), when robots exerted their most disruptive labor-market effects, greater robot exposure significantly slowed growth in both public revenues and expenditures. Revenue losses were driven by declining tax receipts-particularly from individual income, general sales, and corporate income taxes-reflecting an erosion of the tax base rather than adjustments in statutory tax rates. On the expenditure side, robot exposure raised spending on unemployment insurance and welfare assistance programs, while reducing intergovernmental transfers to local governments and public spending on higher education. These adverse fiscal effects weaken in later years as labor markets adjust to automation, with some evidence of modest positive effects on tax revenues. Taken together, our findings suggest that while industrial robots temporarily generated fiscal pressures during the 2000s, they are unlikely to pose a substantial longrun threat to the fiscal sustainability of U.S. states.

title: Rate Channeling Through Deposit Menus

detail.title: Rate Channeling Through Deposit Menus
detail.abstract: A large literature shows that deposit-rate pass-through is incomplete and weaker in concentrated markets, while a parallel literature shows that large banks often post nearly uniform deposit rates across geographies. This paper argues that both facts survive once deposit pricing is treated as a menu of contracts rather than a single rate. Using proprietary deposit-rate data used by banks for competitive benchmarking, I show that market concentration shapes monetary transmission through rotation of the deposit menu rather than uniform attenuation of a representative rate. Vanilla rates serve as inert anchors, but concentration reshapes the rest of the menu: competitive offers move less, screening premia widen, and relative prices within the same bank diverge across markets. The strongest evidence is that concentration weakens the local competitive frontier rather than simply inducing larger unilateral markdowns by the focal bank. These pricing distortions have real consequences for liability composition and profitability during tightening cycles.

title: The Poet as Biological Language Model: On the Structural Resemblance Between Poetic Composition and Large Language Model Inference

detail.title: The Poet as Biological Language Model: On the Structural Resemblance Between Poetic Composition and Large Language Model Inference

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests. The views expressed in this paper are the author’s own.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or experimental interventions requiring ethics approval. It is a conceptual and interpretive analysis based on publicly available ideas, literary theory, and the author’s own analytical framework.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes a novel structural framework for understanding the interaction between human cognition and Large Language Models (LLMs) by drawing a rigorous analogy to formal poetic composition. Moving beyond metaphors such as “stochastic parrots” or “compression algorithms,” it identifies four shared dimensions between the skilled poet and autoregressive inference: (1) corpus formation, comparing experiential training data to textual datasets; (2) constrained generation, mapping prosodic requirements such as meter and rhyme onto sampling parameters such as temperature and top-p; (3) emergent semantics, analyzing how meaning arises bottom-up from formal constraints rather than top-down intent; and (4) the verifier function, equating the “poetic ear” with alignment and oversight mechanisms. The paper does not claim common mechanism, equivalence of cognition, or identity of intention between human and machine; rather, it advances a structural analogy intended to clarify how constrained generative systems produce, test, and refine meaning. It argues that “hallucinations” are not unique to artificial neural networks but are a general property of constrained generative systems—what poets recognize as the “false note.” By synthesizing 20th-century Russian Formalist theory with 21st-century transformer architecture, the paper proposes a “Poetic Posture” for AI governance. It concludes that effective AI alignment is not purely an engineering problem but an epistemological one, requiring a shift toward an apprenticeship model of calibrated trust in which the human operator reclaims the role of the unified generator and verifier.

Keywords: Large Language Models (LLMs), AI Alignment, Human-AI Collaboration, Generative AI, Poetics, Epistemology, AI Governance, Emerging Technologies

detail.abstract: AI systems now drive operational decisions in global grain supply chains, yet no jurisdiction requires enterprises to prove who decided what, when, and on what basis. This paper identifies a "four-layer accountability void": (1) a definition void, where concepts such as algorithmic collusion lack stable application to AI; (2) a regulatory void, where the EU AI Act, CFTC, and China's algorithmic governance each fail to classify grain trading AI as a subject of oversight; (3) an enforcement void, with zero publicly reported regulatory actions worldwide; and (4) a precedent void, with no court judgment or arbitration award on point. Through comparative analysis across seven jurisdictions and scenario-based stress testing, the paper documents how major trading houses have deployed AI while no regime exists for decision-level accountability. The analysis is diagnostic, intended to define the problem for regulators, legal scholars, and industry participants.

title: Reserve Demand Estimation with Minimal Theory
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Department of Economics and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond

detail.title: Reserve Demand Estimation with Minimal Theory
detail.abstract:
We propose a new reserve-demand estimation strategy---a middle ground between atheoretical reduced-form econometric approaches and fully structural quantitative-theoretic approaches. The strategy consists of an econometric specification that satisfies core restrictions implied by theory and controls for changes in administered-rate spreads that induce rotations and shifts in reserve demand. The resulting approach is as user-friendly as existing reduced-form econometric methods but improves upon them by incorporating a minimal set of theoretical restrictions that any reserve demand must satisfy. We apply this approach to U.S. data and obtain reserve-demand estimates that are broadly consistent with the structural estimates.

detail.title: Inequality and Intergenerational Mobility in Sierra Leone

contentType.other: Working Paper submitted to Journal of African Economies

publicationDetails.detailsText: This is the original version of the paper, currently under review at the Journal of African Economies.

detail.abstract: This paper provides the first comprehensive microdata-based assessment of inequality of opportunity and intergenerational mobility in Sierra Leone. Using the 2003 and 2018 Sierra Leone Integrated Household Surveys and focusing on consumption and education, we combine an ex-ante parametric approach with conditional inference trees, random forests, and Shapley-value decompositions to isolate the share of inequality attributable to predetermined circumstances such as birthplace, parental education and occupation, gender, and religion. The inequality of consumption is high (Gini 0.34), and about 55% of it is explained by circumstances, with birthplace and mothers' occupations emerging as the main contributors. A cohort-based analysis aligned with key historical periods shows strong increases in literacy, especially among younger and female cohorts, and a marked decline in literacy-related inequality of opportunity, although regional and gender gaps persist. Transition matrices and two-sample two-stage least squares estimates of intergenerational elasticity and rank-rank slopes indicate moderate but non-trivial persistence in living standards, schooling, and occupational status, with immobility particularly pronounced at the top and bottom of the distributions. In general, the results suggest that recent education reforms have expanded opportunities, but that gender and place-sensitive policies remain essential to reduce circumstance-driven disparities and accelerate upward mobility.

detail.abstract: As of 2024, women's participation in India's workforce was 28.69% (ILO). In 2025, 34% of women were engaged in the IT sector (NASSCOM). Women's representation across all sectors in India is increasing significantly. However, women in the IT sector face multidimensional challenges in their workplaces and families, including inflexible working hours, large tasks with limited time, gender disparity, lower salaries compared to men, and job insecurity. These issues are associated with adverse effects on women's mental health and wellbeing. Married women experience these challenges more acutely due to a lack of work-life balance in the IT sector. The study found that 42% of surveyed women in Chennai's IT sector reported divorce, citing workrelated challenges as a contributing factor. Additionally, the study identified limited mental or emotional support from family members, particularly in their husbands' households, where women are required to manage household chores, childcare, and other responsibilities. This study examines the determinants of mental health and wellbeing among women in the IT sector in Chennai, Tamil Nadu, using quantitative and qualitative research methodologies. Primary data was collected through a well-structured questionnaire from TCS, Wipro, Tech Mahindra, and HCL. The study recommends adopting an AI-powered "Never Alone" program, designed to provide mental health support through virtual counseling and resources, to improve the mental health of women in IT. Based on its findings, the study also proposes policy recommendations to strengthen the mental health and wellbeing of women in the IT sector, with potential implications for women throughout India.

title: When Does Volatility Model Selection Matter? Entropy Diagnostics and Pre-Registered Evidence Across 1,496 Assets and Eleven Asset Classes

detail.title: When Does Volatility Model Selection Matter? Entropy Diagnostics and Pre-Registered Evidence Across 1,496 Assets and Eleven Asset Classes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests.

detail.abstract:
We study when volatility model selection has value, rather than which model wins on average. A single entropy statistic, computable in seconds from a trailing return window, identifies 94% of assets where a simple EWMA baseline suffices—eliminating 86% of model-fitting cost. A 2×2 in-sample attribution separates two mechanisms: filtered historical simulation (FHS) fixes unconditional VaR coverage, while model diversity reduces violation clustering. Walk-forward backtesting across 1,491 assets establishes the paper's central out-of-sample result: per-window best-model selection overfits, but forecast combination (EW-COMB) preserves the Christoffersen clustering benefit (+6.8–8.3 percentage points over EWMA+FHS, p < 10⁻¹¹). Model selection does not improve out-of-sample volatility forecasting or generate position-sizing alpha, bounding the framework's value to computational triage, regime diagnostics, and OOS violation-clustering reduction via forecast combination.

The framework evaluates twelve volatility forecasters across a 1,496-asset, 11-class cross-asset universe with twelve pre-registered hypotheses, cryptographic spec-locking, and hash-chained computation records. Nine hypotheses pass after multiple-testing corrections; three null results are reported with equal rigor. Twenty-eight supplementary analyses (S1–S28) are released as an extensible interface against the benchmark's immutable SQLite data store, enabling researchers to test new hypotheses without modifying the core pipeline or breaking the pre-registration chain.

title: Identifying Uncertainty, Learning about Productivity, and Human Capital Acquisition: A Reassessment of Labor Market Sorting and Firm Monopsony Power
affiliations: Queen Mary University of London, Stanford University - Department of Economics, University College London - Department of Economics and The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: Identifying Uncertainty, Learning about Productivity, and Human Capital Acquisition: A Reassessment of Labor Market Sorting and Firm Monopsony Power
detail.abstract:
We examine the empirical content of a large class of dynamic matching models of the labor market with ex-ante heterogeneous firms and workers, symmetric uncertainty and learning about workers’ productivity, and firms’ monopsony power. We allow workers’ human capital, acquired before and after entry into the labor market, to be general across firms to varying degrees. Such a framework nests and extends known models of worker turnover across firms, occupational choice, wage growth, wage differentials across occupations, firms, and industries, and wage dispersion across workers and over the life cycle. We establish intuitive conditions under which the model primitives are semiparametrically identified solely from data on workers’ wages and jobs, despite the dynamics of these models giving rise to complex patterns of selection based on endogenously time-varying observable and unobservable characteristics of workers and firms. By relying on this identification argument, we develop a constructive estimator of the model primitives, which builds on common methods for mixture and extremal quantile regression models and displays standard properties. Through the lens of this framework, we investigate how well typical empirical wage measures of matching assortativeness and firms’ wage-setting power detect the degrees of sorting and monopsony power in the labor market, respectively. We show that usual measures of sorting severely understate its importance because they ignore the option value of worker human capital and the information about worker productivity acquired through employment, in terms of higher future wages and improved future sorting, which is priced into current wages thus depressing them. We also demonstrate how the markdown of wages relative to output largely overstates firms’ labor market power by ignoring that this option value, which captures future returns from acquired human capital and information, generally lowers wages. We find evidence of both of these features in U.S. data by documenting a strong degree of labor market sorting once appropriately measured and, correspondingly, a lower degree of firm monopsony power than typically documented.

title: Visual Guide to "Quantum Cognition Pricing Theory" (Presentation Slides)

detail.title: Visual Guide to "Quantum Cognition Pricing Theory" (Presentation Slides)
detail.abstract:
This slide deck provides a concise visual overview of the Quantum Cognition Pricing Theory (QCPT). Created to enhance accessibility for a broader audience, this presentation serves as a structured roadmap to a proposed paradigm in asset pricing. It establishes a complete framework grounded in eight postulates, systematically formulating price formation as a computable cognitive process that bridges psychological perception and physical market observation through the principles of quantum statistics.

The slides walk through the implementation of the Quantum Cognition Pricing Model (QCPM)—the first realized instance of this theory—which has demonstrated superior predictive performance over classical time series and machine learning benchmarks across global indices (KOSPI 200, Nasdaq 100, and DAX). By distilling the 300-page dissertation into a visual journey, this deck offers a strategic entry point into the QCPT framework and the Quantum Cognition Market Hypothesis (QCMH), inviting interdisciplinary collaboration and strategic partnerships.

title: Oil, Yen, and Fragility: The Carry Trade Domino in a High-Debt Era
affiliations: Chief Editor, Gomdolee

detail.title: Oil, Yen, and Fragility: The Carry Trade Domino in a High-Debt Era
detail.abstract: The global financial system remains vulnerable to geopolitical oil shocks transmitted through currency dynamics and elevated leverage. This paper examines the "oil-yen nexus": disruptions in oil supply (e.g., Strait of Hormuz risks) raise yen-denominated crude costs for Japan, a neartotal importer, prompting Bank of Japan responses that strengthen the yen and trigger a reverse unwind of the yen carry trade. In a world with record $348 trillion global debt (IIF, 2026), moderate oil price increases to $80-90 per barrel-as seen in early March 2026 after U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran-inflict damage comparable to the inflation-adjusted 2007-2008 peaks (~$140-200 in today's terms) due to debt multipliers amplifying imported inflation, margin erosion, and fiscal strain. The core thesis argues that the sequence-oil shock → yen cost surge → BOJ intervention → yen appreciation → carry unwind → liquidity contraction-poses elevated systemic risk in the current high-debt regime, distinguished from prior episodes by a tangible geopolitical catalyst and rebuilt leverage post-2024. Implications include potential 20-40% equity drawdowns, widened credit spreads, and contagion to emerging markets. Policy recommendations focus on energy diversification, macroprudential limits on carry exposures, enhanced central-bank coordination, and technological efficiency gains. This analysis aligns with the current theme of dialogue amid contested global dynamics, offering a forward-looking risk assessment grounded in institutional data and historical analogues.

title: Corporate Tax Avoidance as an Unintended Consequence of Local Government Debt: Evidence from China's 4-Trillion-Yuan Stimulus Plan
affiliations: , Zhejiang University of Finance and Economics and Victoria University of Wellington

detail.title: Corporate Tax Avoidance as an Unintended Consequence of Local Government Debt: Evidence from China's 4-Trillion-Yuan Stimulus Plan
detail.abstract: Using China's 4-Trillion-Yuan Stimulus Plan as a quasi-natural experiment, we examine how local government debt expansion influences corporate tax avoidance. Our empirical results show that doubling the intensity of debt expansion significantly reduces corporate tax avoidance by approximately 1.189 percentage points. Further analysis suggests that the reduction effect is driven by enhanced tax collection and administrative enforcement. In addition, the reduction effect is more significant among firms with weaker internal controls, tighter financing constraints, non-central enterprises, and those operating in industries with less tax avoidance space. These findings indicate that fiscal stress prompts local governments to exercise selective and responsive tax enforcement. This study provides new evidence on the determinants of corporate tax avoidance from the perspective of government debt. The findings suggest that mitigating debt risks requires clearer government-market boundaries and reduced regional tax competition. Achieving a unified national market highlights the need for greater transparency and consistency in fiscal governance.

title: Expected Returns with Trends and Cycles
affiliations: Harvard University - Business School (HBS) and New York University (NYU) - New York University, Abu Dhabi

detail.title: Expected Returns with Trends and Cycles
detail.abstract: We argue that cash flow growth contains a permanent trend component, rendering the price-dividend ratio a noisy proxy for expected returns. Jointly filtering trend growth, cash flow cycles, and expected returns via an Extended Kalman Filter, we show this cash flow noise generates severe attenuation bias in standard predictive regressions. Purging cash-flow trends and cycles restores return predictability, delivering out-of-sample R 2 of 9% at one-year and 22% at five-year horizons, where traditional valuation ratios uniformly fall short. While discount rate variation dominates price-dividend movements at short and medium horizons, trend growth dominates at longer horizons.

title: A Three-Agent DSGE Model with Banking Intermediation and Firm-Specific Capital: Towards an Inclusive Monetary Policy
affiliations: Infrastructure Economics Centre and

detail.title: A Three-Agent DSGE Model with Banking Intermediation and Firm-Specific Capital: Towards an Inclusive Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: This paper develops and estimates a three-agent New Keynesian DSGE model with a banking sector to analyze the transmission of macroeconomic shocks in the Kazakhstan economy. The model combines a three-agent household structure, a banking intermediation sector, and firm-specific capital within a unified framework. Households are divided into savers, borrowers, and liquidity-constrained agents who cannot smooth consumption through credit markets. Firms operate with firm-specific capital, which allows them to make not only production and pricing decisions but also investment decisions. Banks intermediate the transformation of household savings into loans that finance investment. The model is estimated using Bayesian methods on quarterly macroeconomic data for Kazakhstan and is used to quantitatively assess the transmission of macroeconomic shocks. The results show that liquidity-constrained households are the most vulnerable to macroeconomic shocks: their consumption reacts more strongly to adverse conditions, increasing consumption inequality across households. Investment shocks and disruptions in the credit channel generate the most persistent macroeconomic fluctuations. The findings also suggest that monetary policy may be more effective when complemented by macroprudential measures aimed at stabilizing credit cycles.

title: The Brina Gap: A Framework for Identifying Growth Mispricing in Equity Markets
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Brina Gap: A Framework for Identifying Growth Mispricing in Equity Markets
detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Brina Gap, a systematic framework for identifying equity mispricing by comparing two independently derived growth rate estimates: the Fundamental Growth Rate (gf = ROIC × Reinvestment Rate), derived from current financial statement data, and the Market-Implied Growth Rate (g*), derived from a reverse discounted cash flow model applied to the current enterprise value. The arithmetic difference between these estimates — computed without circular dependency — constitutes a forward-looking mispricing signal structurally distinct from traditional valuation measures such as price-to-earnings ratios or earnings-based margin of safety calculations. When combined with an Owner Earnings DCF intrinsic value in a two-dimensional valuation matrix, the Brina Gap enables systematic identification of four investment archetypes: Double Discount, Value Trap, Underestimated Growth, and Expensive Hype. An Earnings Quality Divergence filter is proposed as a reliability gate to suppress distorted signals in acquisition-heavy companies. The framework is tested across ten companies and 57 company-year observations spanning 2015–2025, covering technology, consumer, industrial, and payments businesses. Confirmed positive signals (Meta Platforms, Alphabet) and confirmed negative signals (General Electric, PayPal) demonstrate directional accuracy over multi-year horizons. Five boundary conditions are documented under which the gf formula produces economically meaningless outputs despite numerical validity. The Double Discount quadrant — where both the Gap signal and the Owner Earnings Margin of Safety are simultaneously positive — achieves a 75% directional hit rate excluding Boundary Condition 1 failures. The primary limitation of the current backtest is its restriction to large-cap US equities; the framework's stated primary domain of small and mid-cap stocks, where analyst coverage is thinner and mispricings more persistent, remains to be tested empirically.

detail.abstract: We present a machine learning analysis of income inequality in the United States, examining how educational attainment intersects with gender, race/ethnicity, and geography to shape wage outcomes. Using 85,000 individual records from the 2022 American Community Survey (ACS) Public Use Microdata Sample spanning five states, we train and compare four predictive models-OLS regression, Ridge regression, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting-to predict log-transformed annual wage income. Our best model (Gradient Boosting, R²=0.2126) identifies education level as the single most important predictor of income, followed by hours worked per week and age. Crucially, a fairness audit reveals persistent prediction residuals across demographic groups: the model systematically underestimates income for male and White workers while overestimating for female and Black workers. An Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition finds that approximately 100% of the 19.2% male-female wage gap remains unexplained by measured characteristics-evidence of differential returns to equivalent credentials. These findings demonstrate that higher education, while necessary, is insufficient to close demographic wage gaps.

title: Cash Bail or Cash Back? The Impact of Cash Bail Reform on Unemployment Rates
affiliations: Northwestern University Pritzker School of Law, Colorado College - Department of Economics and Business and Colorado College

detail.title: Cash Bail or Cash Back? The Impact of Cash Bail Reform on Unemployment Rates
detail.abstract: Over the last decade, more than twenty states (and also some smaller jurisdic ons) have changed their pretrial policies to reduce or eliminate the use of monetary bail, to instead favor risk-based assessments when deciding whether a defendant should be jailed before trial. This policy change could have an impact on local unemployment rates, as defendants can return to work. On the other hand, incarcerated individuals are removed from the labor force (and therefore unemployment rates) so we might only see an indirect impact via dependents or other family members with complementary work/income ac vi es. In this paper we use panel data, difference-indifference , and endogenous treatment approaches to es mate the effect at a county level across 35 years. The results show clearly that cash bail reform pays a small but financially significant bonus to unemployment rates, reducing them by 0.1 to 0.2 percent per month and thereby paying cash back to jurisdic ons willing to engage in cash bail reform.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence has entered the most consequential arena of democratic life: the election. Not as a future risk, but as a present operational reality reshaping how campaigns are run, how voters are reached, how narratives are constructed, and how electoral outcomes can be manipulated. The 2024 global super election year, in which over 3.7 billion eligible voters in 72 countries went to the polls, produced the most extensive evidence base yet for understanding AI's impact on democratic processes. That evidence yields a conclusion that is simultaneously reassuring and deeply alarming: the feared AI-driven electoral apocalypse did not materialise in 2024, but the structural conditions for a more profound disruption are being assembled, instrument by instrument, election by election.

This paper examines AI and politics across the full spectrum of their intersection — from the transformation of political campaign architecture through AI-powered war rooms and behavioural micro-targeting, to the weaponisation of synthetic media as a tool of voter suppression and narrative manipulation; from the emergence of cognitive narrative engineering as a disciplined political art, to the documented mechanics of algorithmic influence on voter behaviour; from international case studies of AI-enabled electoral interference in Romania, Slovakia, Taiwan, Turkey, India, and Australia, to the structural democratic risks of algocracy and the Liar's Dividend; and from India's position as the world's most complex electoral AI environment to its unique opportunity for global governance leadership.

The paper introduces three original frameworks: the Synthetic Political Ecosystem (SPE) model, mapping the six interlocking mechanisms through which AI shapes political reality; the Democratic Vulnerability Index (DVI), a conceptual instrument for assessing national exposure to AI-enabled electoral interference; and the Responsible Political AI Charter (RPAC), a five-principle normative framework for ethical AI use in electoral contexts. The paper argues that democracy's relationship with AI is not predetermined — it is a design challenge. The democracies that survive and strengthen through the AI era will be those that treat AI governance in electoral contexts not as a regulatory afterthought, but as a constitutional priority.

title: An Empirical Analysis of the Free Senior High School (SHS) Policy and Its Implications for Gender Parity: A Case Study of the Nzema East District

detail.title: An Empirical Analysis of the Free Senior High School (SHS) Policy and Its Implications for Gender Parity: A Case Study of the Nzema East District
detail.abstract: Despite the policy's success in increasing overall enrollment and reducing financial barriers, gender-specific challenges persist, particularly for female students. This study examines the impact of Ghana's Free Senior High School (Free SHS) policy on promoting gender equity in education, focusing on two senior high schools in the Nzema East District. The study adopts a qualitative approach, using semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis to explore enrollment, retention, and completion rates alongside stakeholders' perceptions. Findings reveal that while the Free SHS policy has significantly improved access for girls, socio-cultural norms, inadequate gender-sensitive infrastructure, and economic challenges continue to impede equity. The research highlights the need for targeted interventions, such as mentorship programs, improved school facilities, and community advocacy, to address these barriers. This study provides critical insights into the Free SHS policy's role in achieving Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 4 and 5, offering recommendations to enhance its effectiveness in fostering gender equity in Ghanaian education.

title: Machine Learning Techniques for Synthetic Data Generation in Energy and Financial Markets
affiliations: Ca Foscari University of Venice - Dipartimento di Economia and Ca Foscari University of Venice - Dipartimento di Economia

detail.title: Machine Learning Techniques for Synthetic Data Generation in Energy and Financial Markets

publicationDetails.detailsText: Ca' Foscari University of Venice, Department of Economics Research Paper Series No. 11/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Department of Economics, Ca' Foscari University of Venice Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The availability of sufficiently large, reliable, and high-quality datasets represents a fundamental prerequisite for quantitative analysis and data-driven decision-making in economics and finance. In practice, however, financial data are often limited, noisy, or subject to restricted access, creating significant empirical constraints for both researchers and practitioners. Recent advances in Generative Machine Learning (GenML) provide promising tools to overcome these limitations by enabling the generation of synthetic data capable of preserving the main statistical features of original data. Despite the rapid diffusion of these techniques, most existing studies focus on replicating stylized facts of financial time series or producing forward-looking simulations, while less attention has been devoted to a systematic assessment of the generative fidelity and generalization capacity of alternative models across different distributional environments. Motivated by this gap, this study provides a comparative evaluation of several Deep Generative Machine Learning (Deep-GenML) families by assessing their ability to reproduce both theoretical statistical distributions and empirical financial and commodity market data. The analysis spans multiple Deep-GenML architectures, distributional settings and market regimes, while also examining model performance under alternative training configurations that reflect varying degrees of data availability. The empirical evidence indicates that deep generative models are capable of accurately reproducing complex distributional features-including heavy tails, asymmetry, and multimodality-across a wide range of scenarios. Overall, the results highlight the potential of deep generative approaches as flexible tools for synthetic data generation and distributional modeling in financial and energy market applications.

detail.abstract: A structured assessment was performed of SynapSense Technologies’ proposed hardware-plus-consumables revenue model for EEG-based objective pain monitoring in U.S. hospitals using SEC filings, vendor product documentation, peer-reviewed EEG and pain biomarker literature, American Hospital Association hospital statistics, and research on hospital procurement and group purchasing organizations. Unit economics were calculated from the provided pricing and cost assumptions, and sensitivity analyses were conducted across utilization (500–3,000 sessions/year), consumable pricing ($8–$12), and COGS variation (±20%). Competitive benchmarking was compiled against point-of-care EEG and monitoring incumbents, and regulatory and procurement pathways were evaluated by reference to existing FDA clearances, De Novo classifications, and hospital contracting precedents. High gross margins and strong per-site lifetime value were indicated under baseline utilization, while adoption feasibility was found to depend most strongly on validated clinical performance, workflow integration, and procurement positioning consistent with sensor pull-through models used by established hospital monitoring technologies.

title: Beyond Bilateralism: Why the United Kingdom Must Align with AfCFTA's Digital Model
affiliations: Leeds Beckett University

detail.title: Beyond Bilateralism: Why the United Kingdom Must Align with AfCFTA's Digital Model
detail.abstract: The United Kingdom was the first external partner to formally support the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) and has assisted AfCFTA's digital trade implementation. However, this engagement should transcend beyond donor-funding and technical assistance. The UK's digital trade instruments with African countries, notably the Nigeria's Enhanced Trade and Investment Partnership, the Trade Logistics Information Pipeline with Kenya, and the bilateral digital provisions of the Kenya Strategic Partnership, operate at the national level and have not been aligned with the AfCFTA Digital Trade Protocol's continental ambitions for digital trade. The UK is therefore visible in Africa's digital ecosystem through its institutional partnerships, but effectively absent from the continental layer because its policy instruments remain confined to individual states. This paper examines three areas of regulatory divergence: divergence between bilateral digital standards and continental protocol requirements; the absence of a continental data adequacy agreement between the UK and Africa and the governance gap between initiatives like TLIP and ADAPT. It then proposes mechanisms for alignment.

title: Reconsidering the Relationship Between Vitoria's and Grotius's Contributions to the International Law and Natural Law Traditions

detail.title: Reconsidering the Relationship Between Vitoria's and Grotius's Contributions to the International Law and Natural Law Traditions
detail.abstract: In light of recent reevaluations of the work of Hugo Grotius, this essay analyzes the respective roles of Francisco de Vitoria and Grotius in the construction of the "Grotian tradition" of international law and human rights. In contrast to conventional accounts which understand the two within a progression, this essay argues that Vitoria and Grotius can alternatively be understood as representing two distinct strains of international law and ethics, forms of which persist to this day. The first is that strain which privileges local governance based on the natural law and which insists that international law must have a moral or equitable valence (represented today by liberal internationalism). The second, competing strain which, with its focus on "neutral" rules of commerce and international order, presumes that it need not have such a valence (essentially, neoliberalism). In the process, this essay examines the role of the natural law in Vitoria's thought, which for him was most often a reason against interference or intervention, not for. The essay also highlights the role of the Eighty Years' War between the Dutch United Provinces and Spain in the development of Grotius's understanding of sovereignty, in contrast to the Thirty Years' War which is given more prominence in conventional accounts. (Note: Originally published in the Journal of Religious Ethics 49, no. 1 (2021). This article was converted to Open Access in March 2026 and is now licensed under CC BY-NC-ND. Confirmation of this status has been received from the publisher.)

title: Algorethics and Neuro-Symbolic Military AI: Ontologies, "Hellscapes," Just War, and Silicon Valley

detail.title: Algorethics and Neuro-Symbolic Military AI: Ontologies, "Hellscapes," Just War, and Silicon Valley
detail.abstract: Algorethics, as described in the Rome Call for AI Ethics (2020), is an overarching field that includes algorithmic accountability, systemic AI governance, value-sensitive design (VSD), responsible AI (RAI), trustworthy AI, explainable AI (XAI), and similar terms, but which puts these subfields in conversation with broader, more historical ethical and moral traditions. This essay evaluates the ways in which ontology-supported neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence (NeSy) addresses algorethics concerns about explainability and transparency in military applications of AI but does not solve the problem of accountability, which in the case of AI may be greater than similar concerns regarding other private defense contractors. Existing conflicts in Ukraine and Sudan and a potential “hellscape” strategy in the Taiwan Strait are discussed, as are recent U.S. military actions in Venezuela and Iran, and the crossover effects among them based on common suppliers of AI-supported drones; in Sudan and parts of Ukraine, the label “hellscape” is already apt. A parallel is drawn between John Ford, SJ’s condemnation of obliteration bombing in World War II and the drone-swarmed “hellscapes” that current military technology makes possible. The dispute between Anthropic and the U.S. Defense Department over usage restrictions is discussed, as is the role of Palantir and its stated commitment to norms of just war. In addition to Ford, the work of Francisco de Vitoria and Alasdair MacIntyre is also brought to bear on the problem.

title: The Intramonth Momentum Cycle
affiliations: The Hong Kong Polytechnic University and Aalto University School of Business

detail.title: The Intramonth Momentum Cycle
detail.abstract: US equity momentum returns accrue almost entirely in just six trading days each month. We show this concentration arises from investors' dash-for-cash: the need to raise cash before month-end payment deadlines leads to selling pressure on loser stocks a few days before month-end. A value-weighted WML strategy invested only during days t−9 to t−4 relative to the last trading day turns $1 into $18.8 over 1980–2025, compared to $2.4 for the rest of the month. The concentration is driven entirely by losers: in stock-level regressions with firm and date fixed effects, bottom-decile losers underperform by an additional 7.2 basis points per day during these six days, while winners show no corresponding pattern. This effect remains stable across subperiods and concentrates among liquid stocks, precisely where institutional liquidity needs would be most visible, suggesting a structural rather than behavioral origin. TAQ data confirm that net selling pressure in losers spikes during the window and reverses at month-start. We achieve causal identification by exploiting the SEC's May 2024 transition to T+1 settlement. This reform eliminated the settlement-mismatch friction and, as predicted, shifted the pre-month-end selling pressure one day later. The timing of momentum crash risk further supports this mechanical view: crashes concentrate at month-start, after the monthly payment cycle has cleared, when loser reversals are the sharpest. Our evidence points to a simple mechanical driver for the momentum premium: systematic month-end liquidity needs financed by selling loser stocks. These findings suggest that momentum is less about slow information diffusion and more about the fundamental plumbing of the equity market.

title: Cost of Debt, Cost of Inequity? Racial Discrimination in the Syndicated Loan Market
affiliations: University of Delaware, University of Miami - Miami Herbert Business School, Syracuse University and University of Delaware - Accounting & MIS

detail.title: Cost of Debt, Cost of Inequity? Racial Discrimination in the Syndicated Loan Market
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the racial and ethnic composition of borrowing firms influences the pricing and structure of syndicated bank loans. Using workforce data from Revelio Labs, we find that firms with higher shares of Black and Hispanic senior employees face higher loan spreads after controlling for credit risk, firm characteristics, and loan terms, while finding no evidence of worse post-loan performance. A one standard deviation increase in senior minority representation is associated with a 5.6 basis point increase in spreads, with stronger effects among firms with limited external financing or closer proximity to lenders. We also find higher upfront fees, higher undrawn spreads, and more concentrated syndicate structures, consistent with adjustments in both pricing and monitoring. The effects weaken when borrowers pair with more diverse lead lenders. Exploiting the 2014–2016 oil price collapse as an exogenous shock to banks’ lending capacity, we show that the relation strengthens among lenders with greater pre-shock exposure to the oil and gas sector.

title: An Artificial-Intelligence-Driven Global Redistribution Channel (AIGRC): A Conceptual Paradigm for the Future of Global Inequality

detail.title: An Artificial-Intelligence-Driven Global Redistribution Channel (AIGRC): A Conceptual Paradigm for the Future of Global Inequality

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human subjects or primary data collection and therefore does not require ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a new macroeconomic concept: the Artificial-Intelligence-Driven Global Redistribution Channel (AIGRC). The framework describes how AI-mediated allocation systems may contribute to large-scale crossborder reallocation of digital capital operating partly outside traditional coordination mechanisms of nation-states and development institutions. While the literature on FinTech, digital financial inclusion, DeFi, and AI-based credit scoring has expanded rapidly, it remains fragmented and largely confined to micro-and meso-level analysis. Existing work does not conceptualize AI-mediated cross-border financial flows as a distinct global redistribution mechanism analogous to established channels such as trade, migration, or official development assistance. The paper develops a foundational conceptual and theoretical framework for this channel. It identifies (i) the origins of capital (global investors and digital platforms), (ii) an AI allocation layer that directs flows using largescale data on needs, risks, and returns, and (iii) digitally connected recipients in low-and middle-income countries. A simple formal model is introduced in which an AI allocation function determines cross-border flows as a function of economic need, expected returns, risk, and algorithmic objectives. The model links the intensity and structure of this AI-driven channel to changes in global inequality via a reduced-form ∆Gini equation. The analysis establishes a novel unit of macroeconomic analysis for studying AI-mediated cross-border redistribution and yields testable comparativestatic predictions about how improvements in digital infrastructure, regulatory constraints, and algorithmic design may amplify or dampen its inequality effects. Rather than providing empirical validation, the paper marks the conceptual emergence of a potential new macroeconomic mechanism with global relevance and outlines a research agenda for forecasting, measuring, and simulating its effects on poverty, inequality, and the political role of nation-states.

title: Energy Price Shock Transmission To Indian Commodity Inflation During The 2026 Iran War
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Energy Price Shock Transmission To Indian Commodity Inflation During The 2026 Iran War
detail.abstract: This study analyses the impact of the 2026 Iran War on Indian commodity prices, focusing on energy and food sectors. Using monthly data (2020-2026) and econometric techniques, including structural break tests and GARCH models, it examines price shocks, passthrough effects, and volatility. Findings show significant oil price transmission to domestic fuel and food prices, with increased postwar volatility. The results provide insights into cost-push inflation in India and offer guidance for policymakers and investors navigating energy-dependent markets.

title: You Say Potato, We Say Legal Issue: Developing the Legal Issues Taxonomy (LIST) for Smarter Issue-Spotting and Access to Justice Infrastructure
affiliations: Stanford Legal Design Lab

detail.title: You Say Potato, We Say Legal Issue: Developing the Legal Issues Taxonomy (LIST) for Smarter Issue-Spotting and Access to Justice Infrastructure
detail.abstract: When people encounter legal problems, they describe them as life problemsabout landlords, debt, family conflict, lost jobs-not as legal issues with formal names and statutory frameworks. This mismatch between how people talk about their problems and how the justice system categorizes them is a fundamental barrier to access to justice. Building technology that bridges this gap requires a shared piece of infrastructure: a comprehensive, machine-readable taxonomy of legal issues, expressed in language that both laypeople and professionals can use. This paper documents the development of the Legal Issues Taxonomy (LIST), a standardized classification of civil legal issues designed to serve as a Rosetta Stone between people's descriptions of their problems and the legal system's categories. 1 LIST was built iteratively from inherited professional taxonomies, expert review, and empirical analysis of how people describe legal problems in online communities. The paper situates the taxonomy development within the broader context of access-to-justice research-drawing on Felstiner, Abel, and Sarat's framework of naming, blaming, and claiming, on legal needs research, and on parallels from public health's digital epidemiology infrastructure. It describes the design principles, construction methodology, expert review process, and empirical evaluation using topic modeling of Reddit legal advice posts. It then traces the taxonomy's evolution from a labeling tool for the Learned Hands crowdsourcing platform into shared infrastructure for a growing ecosystem of AI-powered legal help tools, service directories, and cross-organizational data interoperability. The paper concludes by reflecting on the current landscape of competing legal taxonomies-including LIST, the SALI Legal Matter Specification Standard, and numerous local classification schemes-and argues for systematic crosswalking and data standards infrastructure as a prerequisite for the next generation of access-to-justice technology.

title: Prometheus: An AI-Driven Ethical Decision Support Architecture for Critical Public Sector Environments
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Prometheus: An AI-Driven Ethical Decision Support Architecture for Critical Public Sector Environments

declarations.ethicsApproval: Written consent

detail.abstract: This paper introduces Prometheus, an independent AI-driven decision support architecture designed to assist professionals in high-stakes, time-critical public sector environments. Prometheus addresses a critical and largely unresolved gap in contemporary governance: the absence of structured, ethical and legally accountable decision support for professionals operating under pressure in healthcare, policing, education, defence and public resource management. Prometheus can be implemented on humanoid robots checking and guiding them towards decision making in alignment with human principles and their wellbeing. The system operates in real time, providing contextual guidance, protocol compliance, multi-agency coordination and automatic legal documentation of every decision made. Combined with the Digital Phronesis Practicum (DPP)-a responsible AI user training model developed by the same author-Prometheus constitutes the first integrated framework addressing both the operational and educational dimensions of responsible Human-AI coexistence in critical public sector environments.

title: When Prompts Matter: Quantifying Prompt Uncertainty and Improving Empirical Inference with LLM-Based Measurement
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin - McCombs School of Business

detail.title: When Prompts Matter: Quantifying Prompt Uncertainty and Improving Empirical Inference with LLM-Based Measurement
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to convert text into variables that enter empirical models and decision systems. A central but under-governed design choice in this pipeline is the prompt. Because prompts are cheap to modify, analysts can search over many defensible variants-yet prompt texts are frequently unarchived, complicating replication. We formalize this as prompt uncertainty: variation in measured variables and downstream conclusions induced solely by changing prompt wording while holding the text, model, and decoding fixed. We develop a prompt econometrics framework that treats prompt choice as part of the measurement instrument, introducing a Prompt Instrument Specification (PIS) and admissible prompt family as the unit of documentation. The framework defines promptaveraged estimands under declared governance weights and reports admissible ranges that quantify construct-operationalization uncertainty. For inference, we recommend an items×prompts design with two-way resampling over items and prompts. Across three studies-Kickstarter innovativeness ratings, Amazon review emotion classification, and Stack Overflow answer-quality ratings-equally defensible prompts materially widen uncertainty, shift coefficient magnitudes, and change ranking decisions, even when prompt-to-prompt label flips are rare. In Stack Overflow, model-to-model differences exceed prompt-to-prompt differences, motivating joint governance of prompt and model choice. Our study indicates that LLM-based measurement should be governed as an instrument-archiving the prompt family and reporting prompt-robust sensitivity bands-rather than treated as a fixed preprocessing step.

title: Deterministic Governance Is Multi-Dimensional: Beyond Authorization in AI Systems

detail.title: Deterministic Governance Is Multi-Dimensional: Beyond Authorization in AI Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of FERZ, Inc., a company developing deterministic governance infrastructure for artificial intelligence systems. The concepts discussed in this paper are part of the author's ongoing research and architectural work in this domain. The paper presents a conceptual framework and does not evaluate specific commercial products.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, personal data, or experimental subjects. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence governance is frequently framed as a problem of runtime control, often emphasizing authorization layers that permit or block actions executed by AI systems. While execution authorization is an essential component of governance infrastructure, treating it as the primary or sufficient mechanism for governance obscures deeper architectural requirements.

This paper argues that deterministic governance is inherently multi-dimensional and cannot be reduced to any single control layer. We introduce a five-dimensional framework for deterministic governance consisting of: (1) execution authorization, (2) governance ontology, (3) constraint codification, (4) deterministic decision logic, and (5) proof-carrying decisions. Each dimension addresses a distinct failure mode in the governance of automated decision systems. When any dimension is absent or underdeveloped, governance gaps emerge that cannot be compensated for by strengthening other components.

The paper distinguishes between the logical dependency structure of governance components and their operational enforcement order, clarifying why execution authorization appears at the boundary of action while depending on upstream semantic and logical infrastructure. Particular attention is given to the role of governance ontology in stabilizing policy semantics and to constraint codification as the transformation of policy language into machine-verifiable rule structures.

By articulating governance as a multi-dimensional architectural stack, the framework provides a structured method for evaluating AI governance systems and identifying incomplete or “single-layer” governance approaches. The model therefore offers both a conceptual foundation for deterministic governance and a practical diagnostic tool for organizations deploying high-consequence AI systems in regulated environments.

title: Data-Driven Dashboards for Enhancing Investor Reporting Transparency in American Capital Markets
affiliations: , , ,  and

detail.title: Data-Driven Dashboards for Enhancing Investor Reporting Transparency in American Capital Markets
detail.abstract: The rapid digitalization of financial markets has transformed the way firms communicate information to investors. This study investigates whether data-driven dashboards enhance investor reporting transparency and influence market valuation in U.S. capital markets. Using secondary data from 47 S&P 500 companies across eight sectors, this research applies descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and multiple regression models to evaluate the relationships among digital reporting quality, ESG performance, and market outcomes, as measured by price-to-earnings ratios. The results indicate that companies implementing advanced dashboard-based reporting systems receive significantly higher market valuation premiums. The quality of digital reporting systems shows a strong positive relationship with price-to-earnings ratios (β = 402.97, p < 0.01). Furthermore, the interaction analysis reveals that the valuation impact of ESG performance varies depending on the sophistication of digital transparency infrastructure. Sectoral results show that technology and communication service firms have the most advanced reporting dashboards, while the energy and industrial sectors have stronger ESG scores. These findings highlight the strategic role of digital transparency infrastructure in reducing information asymmetry and improving investor communication. The study contributes to digital transformation research by demonstrating that investor-oriented reporting technologies can generate measurable financial value in capital markets.

title: The Value of Data in the LLM Era: A New Two-Way Complementary Relationship between Model and Data
affiliations: , University of Maryland - Robert H. Smith School of Business and Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business

detail.title: The Value of Data in the LLM Era: A New Two-Way Complementary Relationship between Model and Data
detail.abstract: Data are widely treated as a strategic asset in artificial intelligence, yet their value is often assumed to be intrinsic and model-independent. We challenge this view by arguing that data value in the LLM era is fundamentally model-contingent: the returns to semantically richer data depend on the representational capacity of the model that uses them. We develop a model-data complementarity framework in which the value of semantic granularity increases with model scale and is concentrated in rare, technically complex regions of the data distribution. To test this idea, we construct three versions of a biomedical training corpus-Coarse, Original, and Fine-that systematically vary semantic granularity while preserving underlying clinical facts. We then train two embedding models from distinct capacity regimes, BERT-base (110M) and Qwen3-Embedding-4B, and evaluate them on biomedical retrieval benchmarks. The results show strongly heterogeneous returns to data enrichment. Fine-grained data generate large performance gains for the higher-capacity model but only limited or even negative returns for the smaller model. Mechanism analysis further shows that these gains are concentrated in semantically difficult entities, measured by entity-level perplexity. Finally, under a fixed enrichment budget, targeted semantic enrichment in high-difficulty regions substantially outperforms random enrichment for the larger model, while yielding much smaller gains for the smaller model. Together, these findings reconceptualize data value as emerging from the complementarity between semantic precision and model capacity, and imply that effective data strategy requires aligning data enrichment with the scale of the deployed model.

title: Distraction or Immersion? Investigating the Effect of Internet Memes on User Knowledge Acquisition Behavior in Online Reading
affiliations: Communication University of China, Southern University of Science and Technology, University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business and Southern University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Distraction or Immersion? Investigating the Effect of Internet Memes on User Knowledge Acquisition Behavior in Online Reading
detail.abstract: Users increasingly rely on social media to acquire scientific and health-related knowledge, yet sustaining engagement with expert-driven content remains challenging. Although Internet memes are widely used in digital communication, their role in knowledge consumption is theoretically ambiguous: memes may distract users by increasing cognitive load or foster immersion by enhancing affective engagement. Drawing on cognitive load theory and cognitive absorption, this study examines how embedding memes into online health content shapes users' knowledge acquisition behavior. Using large-scale data from a major health communication account on WeChat and a causal machine learning framework with instrumental variables, we identify a robust nonlinear relationship between meme usage and article completion. Specifically, meme usage exhibits a U-shaped effect: limited meme use reduces completion, whereas more intensive integration increases the likelihood that users read an article to completion. This pattern is systematically shaped by meme design and content characteristics. Thematic relevance mitigates the disruptive effects of low meme usage by reducing extraneous cognitive load, while humor independently enhances completion through cognitive absorption. The effects are further amplified in longer articles and emotionally demanding contexts, such as infectious disease content. Theoretical contributions and managerial implications are discussed.

title: The Cost of Affordance Misalignment: Evidence from a Video Incentive Policy on Social Sharing Platforms
affiliations: Communication University of China,  and The University of Texas at Dallas, Jindal School of Management

detail.title: The Cost of Affordance Misalignment: Evidence from a Video Incentive Policy on Social Sharing Platforms
detail.abstract: As short-form videos reshape digital content ecosystems, many image-or text-centric social platforms have introduced video incentive policies to accelerate their transition toward video-oriented content. While such policies are intended to stimulate creator participation, their downstream consequences for audience remain largely unexplored. Drawing on the affordance lens, we argue that video incentive policies introduce an exogenous shift in a platform's algorithmic affordances. This shift triggers visibility-driven strategic production on the supply side while creating misalignment between video content affordances and users' needs on the demand side, ultimately weakening user engagement. We examine a quasi-natural experiment on RedNote, a leading image-centric social sharing platform that implemented a comprehensive video incentive policy in August 2020. Despite increased exposure and platform-level promotion of video content, we find that user engagement declined following the policy. Specifically, the number of likes and bookmarks on video posts decreased by 17.71% and 16.93%, respectively. To validate the proposed mechanism, we employ large language models (LLMs) to operationalize content-tone congruence. The results show that the policy induced creators to produce more videos that are misaligned with the platform's prevailing tone. Topic modeling of LLM-generated rationales further illustrates shifts in content affordances: the proportions of the "Practical How-To Guides" and "Authentic Product Reviews" decline significantly after the policy. Moreover, heterogeneity analyses reveal that creators with stronger image concerns respond more cautiously to the policy and do not experience post-policy declines in engagement. We further rule out an alternative explanation based on declining video quality due to quick content production. Together, these findings 2 highlight unintended consequences of user-generated content (UGC) incentivization and offer new insights into video content dynamics, algorithmic affordances, and platform ecosystem design.

title: AEGIS: Agent Execution Governance and Integrity Standard — A Survey and Reference Architecture for AI Agent Action Accountability

detail.title: AEGIS: Agent Execution Governance and Integrity Standard — A Survey and Reference Architecture for AI Agent Action Accountability

detail.abstract: As organizations deploy AI agents to execute tasks in business processes, to our knowledge, no systematic academic framework exists for recording, verifying, and ensuring accountability for their actions. This study surveys industrial challenges and regulatory trends in AI agent action recording, formalizes a threat model (T1–T8), and constructs a seven-dimension evaluation framework (D1–D7). Through systematic survey of 20 academic papers and 5 industry projects and comparison matrix analysis, it identifies research gaps and demonstrates the non-substitutability of architectural differences against the two closest existing works (PROV-AGENT, InALign). The survey confirms that "a cryptographically verifiable, independent third-party recording standard for AI agent runtime behavior across platforms" remains an open research problem not addressed by the surveyed works. This paper proposes AEGIS (Agent Execution Governance and Integrity Standard), a three-layer reference architecture targeting these requirements, and evaluates it through a reference implementation across metrics M1–M6 and scenarios S1–S5.

title: Sentiment-Driven Forecasting of Fractional Trading Activity Using LSTM Networks
affiliations: HTW Berlin, HTW Berlin, Berlin School of Economics and Law and University of Applied Sciences for Engineering and Economics (HTW Berlin), School of Computing, Communication and Business

detail.title: Sentiment-Driven Forecasting of Fractional Trading Activity Using LSTM Networks
detail.abstract: Fractional trading has emerged as an opportunity for investors to invest in fractions of shares, enabling access in high-priced stocks even with small budgets, and thus reaching a bigger investment community. Aside from the inventory risk faced by all market makers, providers of fractional trading are unable to perfectly hedge their positions and therefore need to forecast retail investors' order flow over short time horizons to manage their market risk. We develop machine learning models to predict trading activity in fractional trading using time series data on investor holdings of more than 8,000 securities combined with daily news sentiment indicators. Our approach proceeds in two stages. First, securities are grouped into clusters with similar trading patterns, and representative firms are selected from each cluster. Second, trading activity is modeled using long short-term memory (LSTM) neural networks augmented with sentiment features. The results show that fractional trading activity can be modeled with meaningful predictive accuracy and that incorporating news sentiment improves LSTM performance in most cases. Feature importance analysis using methods from explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) identifies the primary drivers of trading activity.

title: Psychological Categories in AI Safety Evaluation: Institutionalization, Validation, and Platform Governance Risk

detail.title: Psychological Categories in AI Safety Evaluation: Institutionalization, Validation, and Platform Governance Risk
detail.abstract:
As generative AI systems become increasingly social and are used in more private, emotionally meaningful contexts, companies have begun to introduce psychological categories such as “mental health” and “emotional reliance” into model safety evaluation. This paper examines how such categories are being formalized in OpenAI’s public safety communications and successive GPT-5-series system cards. The central concern, it argues, is not whether emotionally significant AI use can ever be harmful, but whether broad psychological risk categories are being operationalized, benchmarked, and expanded before their conceptual and empirical foundations have been adequately clarified.

To investigate this question, the paper combines four layers of analysis: OpenAI’s own safety documentation, large-scale empirical evidence on ordinary ChatGPT use, a small exploratory audit of cross-version implementation drift, and historical parallels from digital platform governance. Taken together, these materials suggest that while such categories may not be misguided in principle, their current public formalization remains methodologically under-specified and difficult to independently validate. The broader risk, therefore, is not only potential misclassification in individual cases, but the normalization of an interpretive framework whose conceptual and empirical status remains uncertain.

title: From Tool to Collaborator: Rethinking GIScience as GIS Becomes Agentic and Autonomous
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University and Pennsylvania State University

detail.title: From Tool to Collaborator: Rethinking GIScience as GIS Becomes Agentic and Autonomous
detail.abstract: Geographic Information Systems (GIS) have long been positioned along Wright, Goodchild and Proctor's influential continuum of GIS as a tool, GIS as toolmaking, and GIScience, an arrangement that presumes GIS is epistemically passive and primarily executes human authored intent. This paper argues that the integration of generative AI into GIS introduces functional autonomy in goal interpretation, workflow and code generation, execution monitoring, and iterative revision, which increasingly breaks this boundary condition. Through an integrative narrative review of AI-enabled, agentic, and autonomous GIS, we trace a migration of intent from expert driven command execution toward partial delegation of planning and procedural assembly to systems operating in iterative loops. Building on this analysis, we propose the Agentic Role Entanglement (ARE) model, which replaces the tool-toolmaking-science continuum with an epistemic action loop in which tool use, toolmaking, and epistemic inquiry become dynamically coupled within a single episode. ARE model yields falsifiable implications for evaluation and peer review, motivating a shift from output checking to episode level validation. To support this shift, we outline a layered validation stack centered on provenance, reproducibility, workflow and code verification, geospatial sanity checks, and uncertainty bounded claims. We extend these requirements into a lifecycle view of distributed responsibility and ethical governance. We conclude by advocating a post instrumental GIScience that treats human-agent systems, rather than software alone, as the unit of analysis for scientific defensibility, reproducibility, and accountability.

title: The Missing Dimension of Bitcoin Resilience: Transport Decentralization, Communications Continuity, and Monetary Reachability Under Stress

detail.title: The Missing Dimension of Bitcoin Resilience: Transport Decentralization, Communications Continuity, and Monetary Reachability Under Stress
detail.abstract: Bitcoin is widely described as decentralized, censorship-resistant, and robust by design. These characterizations are substantially correct at the levels of issuance, validation, and ledger replication. They remain incomplete at the level of transport. Transactions, blocks, and node messages still depend on communications pathways that can be degraded, censored, concentrated, or disrupted. This paper argues that the next frontier of Bitcoin resilience is transport decentralization. The goal is to reduce dependence on any single communications path so that disruption becomes less decisive. The paper makes five contributions. First, it identifies transport decentralization as a distinct and under-theorized dimension of Bitcoin resilience-under-theorized specifically as a monetary and institutional category, not as a technical one-alongside ledger, validation, and mining decentralization. It reframes resilience not as invulnerability but as non-decisive disruption and graceful degradation, and directly addresses objections to this framing. Second, it develops the concept of monetary reachability. This is the practical ability of value-bearing information to travel under real communications constraints. It distinguishes monetary reachability from both network reachability and formal consensus. Third, it proposes a layered continuity architecture combining ordinary internet access, routing hardening, non-terrestrial fallback, local relay capacity, and storeand-forward survivability. Fourth, it presents the Bitcoin Transport Resilience Index (BTRI) as an analytic scaffold with operationalized measurement dimensions for each component. Fifth, it explores the BTRI dimensions for Nigeria as a case of high Bitcoin adoption meeting high transport fragility, illustrating how the framework generates a diagnostic profile, and draws implications for financial inclusion and central bank digital currency design. The contribution is synthetic and programmatic. It organizes scattered resilience tools under one coherent doctrine of monetary continuity under stress and outlines a research agenda for engineers, researchers, and policymakers.

title: Citizenship, Recognition and belongings: An insight from Karen's lived experiences in Myanmar
affiliations: Mahidol University - Institute of Human Righs and Peace Studies and Mahidol University - Institute of Human Righs and Peace Studies

detail.title: Citizenship, Recognition and belongings: An insight from Karen's lived experiences in Myanmar
