detail.title: Risk-Adjusted Performance of Diversification Strategies Across Macroeconomic Regimes

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding

detail.abstract: Risk-Adjusted Performance of Diversification Strategies Across Macroeconomic Regimes his paper investigates the risk-adjusted performance of traditional diversification strategies across contrasting macroeconomic regimes. I compare a concentrated S&P 500 portfolio against a diversified portfolio comprising equities, short-term Treasury bills, and gold. The analysis focuses on three market downturns: the Global Financial Crisis (2007), the COVID-19 Pandemic (2020), and the Inflationary Bear Market (2022). Using daily price data, I compute period returns, maximum drawdowns, and annualized Sharpe and Sortino ratios (scaled by ×252 from daily values). Results indicate that diversification improves recovery-window performance in deflationary crises, while inflationary shocks still produce weak risk-adjusted outcomes despite reduced drawdowns.

title: Understanding the Convolutional Neural Network's Stock Return Predictability
affiliations: Brandeis University - International Business School, Brandeis University and

detail.title: Understanding the Convolutional Neural Network's Stock Return Predictability
detail.abstract: Jiang, Kelly, and Xiu (2023) demonstrate that a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on stock price chart images achieves striking out-of-sample return predictability. Building on their framework, this paper aims to understand the origin of the CNN's predictive power. We investigate which visual elements drive the CNN's predictions, whether richer image content can improve them, and where the model focuses its attention within the image. Using controlled ablation experiments, we establish a clear hierarchy among image elements: OHLC (open-high-low-close) price geometry is the dominant source of predictive power, the moving average line is redundant, and volume bars contribute marginally. We further show that augmenting images with 52-week high-low price anchors, grayscale price-level channels, or market index overlays uniformly degrades performance — a "less is more" result indicating that the CNN's optimal input is the parsimonious OHLC representation. Gradient-based saliency maps reveal that the CNN concentrates attention on closing prices near daily high-low extremes in the most recent trading days, with volume spikes as secondary cues. Comparing saliency patterns across image designs uncovers a novel attention-performance paradox: more focused attention is associated with worse out-of-sample performance, while broader, more diffuse scanning of the OHLC geometry yields superior predictions. Our baseline long-short strategy achieves an annualized Sharpe ratio of 3.744 over 2020-2024, confirming that CNN-based predictability remains robust after the original sample period of the paper.

title: Enhancing Tomorrow Education through the Implementation of the Education 4.0 Calculator Learning Method: A Case Study at Phor Tay Secondary School, Malaysia
affiliations: PCET Multimedia Education

detail.title: Enhancing Tomorrow Education through the Implementation of the Education 4.0 Calculator Learning Method: A Case Study at Phor Tay Secondary School, Malaysia
detail.abstract:
Introduction: A workshop focused on implementing the Education 4.0 Calculator Learning Method was conducted at Phor Tay Secondary School in Penang, Malaysia, on October 23, 2023. The primary objective of this workshop was to evaluate the efficacy of the Education 4.0 Calculator Learning Method in the context of secondary education.

Method: The workshop was structured into two distinct parts. The first segment introduced fundamental concepts, including Peter Chew's Rule, Method, and triangle diagrams. The second segment cantered on the Education 4.0 Calculator Learning Method, which was complemented by the utilization of advanced tools like Mathportal ,Wolfram Alpha and Symbolab to provide a comparative perspective.

Results: The implementation of the Education 4.0 Calculator Learning Method during the workshop proved to be highly successful. Significantly, five out of six participating teachers admitted to having no prior knowledge of Peter Chew's Rule, Method, and Triangle Diagram prior to the workshop. This lack of knowledge had previously hindered their ability to efficiently solve all triangle-related problems simple, just need to use one rule and only once. However, following the workshop, all participants expressed increased confidence in their ability to solve all triangle-related problems simple, just need to use one rule and only once. One teacher did have prior knowledge of Peter Chew's Rule, Method, and Triangle Diagram, enabling her to solve all triangle-related problems simple, just need to use one rule and only once even before the workshop. All six teachers unanimously endorsed the integration of Peter Chew's Triangle Diagram and the Education 4.0 Calculator Learning Method into the Malaysian Ministry of Education's Additional Mathematics curriculum. This integration is expected to enhance the teaching and learning of Solution of Triangle Topics (KSSM, Level 4), ultimately leading to more effective educational outcomes.

Conclusion: This study highlights the transformative impact of the Education 4.0 Calculator Learning Method at Phor Tay Secondary School. Moreover, all six teachers found Peter Chew's Method and Rule to be more accessible and effective compared to conventional approaches when solving triangle-related problems. The Educational 4.0 Calculator was recognized as a user-friendly tool that significantly enhances the teaching and learning of Solution of Triangle Topics (KSSM, Level 4). These findings underscore the potential for innovative educational methods and tools to revolutionize the teaching and learning experience.

title: Energy Sanctions Hegemony
affiliations: University of Houston Law Center

detail.title: Energy Sanctions Hegemony
detail.abstract:
While the United States leverages its global financial dominance to deploy unilateral energy sanctions as a primary economic tool, these sanctions create an impossible dilemma for U.S. energy companies: comply with sanctions and breach foreign contractual obligations or honor their contractual obligations and face prosecution at home. This extraterritorial assertion of regulatory power systematically undermines the foundational principles of contract law, disrupting energy contracts while trapping companies between irreconcilable compliance demands.

Theoretically, contract law offers an escape route: parties can invoke doctrinal principles such as frustration or illegality to extricate themselves from the contractual impossibilities; however, this Article challenges that notion. It contends that these common law doctrines consistently fail to provide meaningful relief because courts across multiple jurisdictions routinely reject unilateral energy sanctions as grounds for contract discharge. This pattern of judicial hostility toward sanctions-based defenses reveals the structural inadequacy of traditional contract doctrines to address sanctions-induced disruptions. It exposes a fundamental tension: the United States asserts hegemonic regulatory power while foreign courts repudiate that power, trapping companies between irreconcilable legal obligations.

Rather than relying on inadequate common law doctrines, this Article proposes a dual approach. It argues for recalibrating sanctions imposition to account for energy sanctions-induced contractual disruptions while advancing innovative contractual hedging strategies to preserve commercial obligations.

The Article makes three novel contributions to legal scholarship. First, it conceptualizes energy sanctions hegemony and demonstrates the coercive capacity of unilateral sanctions to undermine contractual certainty and legal predictability. Second, it reveals the doctrinal inadequacy of common-law remedies in resolving the tension between the U.S. assertion of extraterritorial energy sanctions authority and the judicial rejection of that authority, demonstrating how this tension traps U.S. companies. Third, it offers concrete solutions through "contractual hedging" and innovative drafting strategies, including a bifurcated governing-law provisions.

title: Examining the Energy and Environmental Footprint of Data Centers in India
affiliations: Power Management Institute India and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Examining the Energy and Environmental Footprint of Data Centers in India
detail.abstract: This study develops one of the first integrated, national-scale assessments of the energy and environmental footprint of India's rapidly expanding data center ecosystem through 2035. Using a scenario-based modelling framework, we project infrastructure growth under three demand pathways-Conservative, Base, and Optimistic-combined with alternative assumptions on power usage effectiveness (PUE: 1.6-1.2), grid decarbonization trajectories (Business-as-Usual and Net Zero Emissions 2050), and water-efficiency multipliers (1.0-0.6). Results indicate that the number of operational facilities could reach 376-532 by 2035, driving electricity demand from 2.66 GW in 2025 to 25-42 GW by 2035, with annual energy consumption rising from 23 TWh to 219-372 TWh-equivalent to 6-14% of projected national electricity use. Under a BAU pathway, operational emissions increase from 15 MTCO₂ in 2025 to 112-191 MTCO₂ by 2035, while water withdrawals rise from 0.13 BCM to 1.25-2.12 BCM. Although efficiency improvements and grid decarbonization moderate intensity metrics, absolute impacts increase sharply, revealing a scale-sustainability paradox. Spatial analysis reveals persistent clustering in Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, and Delhi NCR, intensifying localized grid and water stress. The findings underscore the urgency of renewable procurement, advanced cooling technologies, spatial diversification, and coordinated grid planning to align India's digital expansion with longterm sustainability objectives.

title: Temporal Focus and Stock Price Reactions to Earnings Calls
affiliations: Stockholm Business School, Stockholm University, University of Zurich - Department of Finance and University of Zurich

detail.title: Temporal Focus and Stock Price Reactions to Earnings Calls
detail.abstract: We study the stock market consequences of managerial focus on the future versus the past, "Future minus Past (FMP)," in earnings conference calls. FMP is accompanied by more positive tone, suggesting it should also boost the stock price. Surprisingly, we find that stock prices respond negatively to FMP in presentations. Rationalizing the puzzling effect on stock returns, FMP in presentations is associated with higher return volatility, bid-ask-spreads, forecast dispersion, and forecast errors. Thus, focusing on the future in earnings call presentations appears to leave investors more confused, rather than informed. In contrast, FMP in answers to the analyst questions decreases uncertainty and stock price reactions are generally positive, suggesting that when prompted by analysts, FMP provides information. Overall, the context in which information is presented influences how investors and analysts interpret the same linguistic feature.

title: Scoring Intensity Under Competing Termination Risks: A Modular Point Process Framework

detail.title: Scoring Intensity Under Competing Termination Risks: A Modular Point Process Framework
detail.abstract: We introduce the Discounted Scoring Framework (DSF), a modular point process framework that integrates scoring intensity with competing termination risks. Its components, including possession indicators, period/game survival functions, and inter-period boundary conditions, assemble to match the rule structure of a given sport. Traditional models treat game duration as a fixed boundary; the DSF instead discounts expected scoring by the joint survival probability of period and game continuation. Two-staged estimation combines maximum likelihood for scoring intensity with Cox and Breslow methods for termination hazard. Simulations across eleven sport configurations validate consistent parameter recovery, while empirical applications to NHL, MLB, and UFC data demonstrate tight calibration and stable out-of-sample generalization. Assembling fitted MLB components into the full expected score integral produces game-level predictions consistent with observed scoring averages. The framework supports principled over/under market making, high-frequency live event prediction, and analysis of prospective rule changes on marginal scoring rates.

title: The Fast Lane Keyword Methodology: A Structural Framework for Identifying and Prioritizing Zero-Data Long-Tail Keywords in Competitive Digital Markets

detail.title: The Fast Lane Keyword Methodology: A Structural Framework for Identifying and Prioritizing Zero-Data Long-Tail Keywords in Competitive Digital Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Global Marketing Director at NP Digital, the company that owns and operates Ubersuggest and AnswerThePublic, the platforms referenced in this paper. The Fast Lane Keyword Methodology was developed from operational experience managing keyword research strategy for these platforms. This practitioner perspective is disclosed as the source of the empirical examples and operational insights presented. The author has no financial interest in the commercial adoption of the methodology beyond its general contribution to the effectiveness of the platforms' user base.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, patients, or identifiable personal data. The empirical examples are drawn from publicly accessible search engine results pages and keyword research tools. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently by the author based on operational experience at NP Digital.

detail.abstract: Contemporary keyword research methodology relies heavily on aggregated search volume data from tools such as DataForSEO, Ahrefs, and SEMrush to identify content opportunities. This reliance creates a systematic blind spot: queries that fall below the aggregation threshold of these platforms-returning zero volume, zero keyword difficulty, and zero cost-per-click-are routinely dismissed as non-opportunities. This paper argues that this dismissal is structurally mistaken and disproportionately harmful to small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) and solopreneurs who lack the domain authority and content budgets required to compete on high-volume terms. Drawing on operational experience managing keyword strategy for AnswerThePublic and Ubersuggest at NP Digital-platforms collectively generating between 50 and 200 unique query variants per keyword search across 190+ country markets-this study proposes the Fast Lane Keyword Methodology: a four-signal structural scoring framework that assigns prioritization scores (0-12) to zero-data queries based on word count, intent modifier presence, SERP competition weakness, and semantic parent alignment. The central argument is that zero data does not indicate zero demand; it indicates zero competition from large publishers, creating a structural first-mover advantage that is disproportionately accessible to smaller content producers. Theoretical implications for long-tail keyword theory and practical applications for SMB content strategy are discussed.

title: Foreign Tax Credits and Global Minimum Tax: Policy Challenges in Preventing Double Taxation for Multinational Enterprises

detail.title: Foreign Tax Credits and Global Minimum Tax: Policy Challenges in Preventing Double Taxation for Multinational Enterprises
detail.abstract: The increasing globalization of business activities has intensified challenges in international corporate taxation, particularly in preventing double taxation of cross-border income. The introduction of the OECD’s Global Minimum Tax under the Pillar Two framework represents a significant development in international tax policy aimed at ensuring that multinational enterprises (MNEs) pay a minimum level of tax on their global profits. At the same time, the U.S. Foreign Tax Credit (FTC) system has historically served as a key mechanism to mitigate double taxation on foreign-source income. This paper examines the interaction between the FTC regime and the OECD Pillar Two Global Anti-Base Erosion (GloBE) rules, focusing on potential overlaps, compliance challenges, and policy implications. Through a comparative analysis of domestic tax provisions and international tax reforms, the study highlights areas where coordination may be necessary to avoid unintended double taxation. The paper concludes with policy recommendations aimed at improving alignment between domestic tax systems and global minimum tax standards.

title: Global SEO as a Growth Lever: A Framework for International Digital Acquisition in SaaS Products

detail.title: Global SEO as a Growth Lever: A Framework for International Digital Acquisition in SaaS Products

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author serves as Global Marketing Director at NP Digital, the organization responsible for Ubersuggest and AnswerThePublic, the products discussed in this paper.

detail.abstract: The globalization of Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) products has fundamentally altered the competitive landscape of digital marketing, necessitating the development of sophisticated international acquisition strategies. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for leveraging Search Engine Optimization (SEO) as a primary growth lever in international SaaS markets, drawing on empirical insights from the management of two globally recognized digital marketing platforms: Ubersuggest and AnswerThePublic, both part of NP Digital's product portfolio. Through analysis of cross-market user behavior data, content localization strategies, and growth hacking methodologies applied across multiple geographic regions, this study identifies critical success factors for scaling SaaS user acquisition internationally. Our findings demonstrate that culturally adapted SEO strategies, when integrated with data-driven growth frameworks, yield significantly higher user acquisition rates and lower customer acquisition costs (CAC) compared to uniform global campaigns. We propose a three-pillar framework-Market Intelligence, Content Localization, and Growth Loop Engineering-as a replicable model for SaaS organizations pursuing international expansion. Practical implications for digital marketing executives and growth practitioners are discussed.

title: Strategic Alliances between Multinational Corporations and Business Process Outsourcing Firms: Reframing Corporate Social Responsibility through Alliance Innovation Architecture

detail.title: Strategic Alliances between Multinational Corporations and Business Process Outsourcing Firms: Reframing Corporate Social Responsibility through Alliance Innovation Architecture

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declared no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Recent global disruptions have exposed structural weaknesses in how Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) is conceptualised and operationalised within outsourcing alliances. In multinational corporation-business process outsourcing (MNC-BPO) relationships, CSR often remains symbolic and weakly integrated into alliance governance, limiting its influence on innovation and long-term value creation. This paper develops a conceptual framework that repositions CSR as a governance architecture embedded within alliance design. Building on the Triple Win (win-win-win) business approach, the study introduces Alliance Innovation Architecture to explain how ethical responsibility can enable innovation, resilience, and legitimacy across inter-organisational boundaries. The framework integrates insights from strategic alliance theory, governance research, and innovation studies to demonstrate how responsibility-oriented governance shapes learning, coordination, and capability development in outsourcing ecosystems. The paper contributes to theory by reframing CSR as infrastructural rather than voluntary, extending alliance theory beyond firm-centric logics, and advancing a governance-centred understanding of innovation. It offers practical guidance for executives and policymakers seeking to design ethically grounded and innovation-capable alliance systems under conditions of systemic uncertainty.

title: Spatio-Temporal Coupled Optimization and an Improved Genetic Algorithm for the Continuous Berth Allocation Problem
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Spatio-Temporal Coupled Optimization and an Improved Genetic Algorithm for the Continuous Berth Allocation Problem
detail.abstract: To address the inadequate modeling of berth position–operation time coupling in the Continuous Berth Allocation Problem (CBAP), this study proposes a spatio-temporal optimization framework that captures the impact of berth position deviation on operational efficiency while coordinating vessel service performance and quay utilization. A berth position deviation function is embedded into vessel service time to establish a linkage between spatial berth allocation and operational efficiency. A weighted bi-objective model is formulated to minimize the total vessel port time and the berth occupation span. To reduce the subjectivity of weight selection, an adaptive Pareto-based calibration method is developed to determine weight coefficients under congested, normal, and relaxed operational scenarios. To solve the resulting nonlinear and high-dimensional optimization problem, an improved genetic algorithm incorporating elite retention, adaptive mutation, and parallel computing mechanisms is designed. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed model effectively captures the operational impact of berth deviation and improves the spatial–temporal coordination of quay operations. The scenario-adaptive weighting strategy enhances solution robustness under different operating conditions, while the improved genetic algorithm exhibits strong convergence performance and high solution quality for medium-to-large-scale problem instances. Overall, this study advances continuous berth scheduling modeling from a spatio-temporal coupling perspective and provides a novel optimization framework and solution approach that strengthens both the scientific rigor and practical applicability of port scheduling decisions.

title: The Inniss Institute: A New Center for Digital Governance and Intellectual Property in the Caribbean and Global South
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Inniss Institute: A New Center for Digital Governance and Intellectual Property in the Caribbean and Global South
detail.abstract: This policy brief argues that without decisive action, the Caribbean risks remaining a “digital plantation” in the global AI economy—supplying cultural data while receiving little economic, technological, or narrative benefit. It identifies an extraction paradox driven by unregulated data harvesting, expansive foreign fair use doctrines, and limited regional AI capacity. To address this, the brief proposes a four‑pillar strategy for the CARICOM AI Policy Roadmap: rejecting overbroad fair use for AI training, establishing a CARICOM Data Trust, enforcing transparency to protect moral rights, and investing in regional AI infrastructure and talent. Together, these measures position the Caribbean as a sovereign, competitive, and culturally grounded AI actor.

title: Beyond Symbolic CSR: Customer Relationship Management as Strategic Ethical Infrastructure in Inter-Organizational Alliances

detail.title: Beyond Symbolic CSR: Customer Relationship Management as Strategic Ethical Infrastructure in Inter-Organizational Alliances

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declared no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) continues to face a persistent implementation gap, particularly within inter-organizational alliances where ethical commitments diffuse across firm boundaries. While prior research emphasizes normative responsibility and governance design, it offers limited insight into how responsibility becomes structurally embedded in everyday coordination systems. This paper reconceptualizes organizational relational infrastructures-operationalized through Customer Relationship Management (CRM) systems-as strategic ethical governance architecture-a socio-technical governance architecture that embeds accountability, transparency, and stakeholder alignment within alliance relationships. Drawing on institutional theory, stakeholder governance, and alliance research, we develop a conceptual framework explaining how infrastructural embedding reduces CSR decoupling and enhances ethical durability under conditions of institutional complexity and crisis. By shifting attention from voluntarist commitment to governance architecture, the paper advances business and society scholarship and offers a system-level explanation of how responsible value creation can be sustained across organizational boundaries. This paper forms part of a broader research programme examining governance systems, strategic alliances, and ethical infrastructure in complex organizational environments (Bakr, 2023; Bakr, 2026a; Bakr, 2026b; Bakr, 2026d).

title: How Do Past Privacy Choices Shape the Future?
affiliations: University of Toronto

detail.title: How Do Past Privacy Choices Shape the Future?
detail.abstract: Consumers face frequent and consecutive digital privacy choices, but each choice is not necessarily independent. This paper demonstrates that past privacy choices affect consumers' current privacy choices. Such state-dependent choices suggest that privacy choices can have externalities within a platform in which one app's data requests can affect the ability of other apps to collect data. Specifically, I use an individual-level consumer panel to investigate data consent decisions by consumers on Alipay, a major digital platform that connects users and thirdparty apps. Leveraging a natural experiment that encourages users to accept data requests, I find that the probability of rejecting the next request declines 15%. This effect decays over time; it is larger when preferences for the app at that moment are relatively weak, as categorized by large language models (LLMs); and for users whose privacy preferences are relatively weak. The effect does not differ by whether the specific data requested in consecutive data consent decisions is the same. Overall, these results suggest that the externalities arising from state-dependent data consent choices are temporary. Nevertheless, this temporary effect incentivizes platforms to encourage apps to provide consumer-friendly data request designs.

title: When Brakes Accelerate: Braking-Device Inversion in Competitive Technological Races

detail.title: When Brakes Accelerate: Braking-Device Inversion in Competitive Technological Races

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a theory of institutional inversion under competitive technological races. We argue that braking devices-institutional mechanisms designed to restrain dangerous acceleration-do not simply fail under competitive pressure; they undergo a structural transformation into legitimacy mechanisms that authorize continued acceleration. We term this phenomenon braking-device inversion. The argument is formalized through a repeated acceleration-restraint game: under competitive first-mover incentives and irreversibility premia, acceleration becomes a rational dominant strategy even when actors prefer mutual restraint, and the institutions designed to prevent this outcome are endogenously transformed by the same competitive dynamics they were intended to govern. Although the empirical illustrations are drawn from advanced AI development, the theoretical framework applies to any technological race in which capital irreversibility, first-mover advantages, and opacity interact with institutional design. The framework identifies three equilibrium forms. Type A (Lock-In Equilibrium) arises when switching costs exceed a critical threshold, rendering reversal strategically prohibitive. Type B (Governance Capture Equilibrium) emerges when the benefit of endogenous standard-setting surpasses external enforcement capacity. Type C (Cascading Fragility Equilibrium) occurs when increasing coupling and declining stop authority make systemic cascade risk endogenous to architecture. These three equilibrium forms are unified by the mechanism of braking-device inversion: the same competitive pressure that motivates institutional adoption transforms braking devices from operative constraints into legitimating mechanisms for continued acceleration. The paper conceptualizes reversibility, verifiability, and distributedness as equilibrium-shifting parameters that expand the domain in which restraint is incentive-compatible. The argument contributes to the political economy of technological competition by specifying structural conditions under which institutional failure becomes a rational outcome rather than a deviation from it.

title: Leveraged Looping in Digital Real-World Asset Markets
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: Leveraged Looping in Digital Real-World Asset Markets
detail.abstract: The tokenization of real-world assets (RWAs) has emerged as one of the most consequential developments at the intersection of traditional finance and decentralized finance (DeFi). By representing ownership or economic rights in instruments such as government bonds, private credit, and real estate through blockchain-based tokens, tokenization has enabled traditional assets to be integrated into decentralized lending platforms. As these markets have matured, participants have developed increasingly sophisticated yield-enhancement strategies, among the most notable of which is leveraged looping. This recursive yield-amplification technique involves depositing tokenized RWAs as collateral, borrowing stablecoins against that collateral, and reinvesting the borrowed funds to purchase additional RWA tokens. Through successive iterations, investors create and expand leveraged exposure to the underlying asset's yield while maintaining the same initial capital. This paper examines the mechanics and economic rationale of leveraged looping strategies, analyzes the structural risks arising from the integration of traditional financial assets into decentralized financial infrastructure, and evaluates the regulatory and financial stability implications of these strategies. Particular attention is directed toward the mismatch between the continuous operation of DeFi platforms and the slower settlement, valuation, and liquidity characteristics of the underlying assets. The analysis draws on recent market data, protocol-level case studies, and relevant academic literature. The paper concludes that leveraged looping represents a technologically innovative adaptation of traditional leverage and carry-trade strategies but may introduce new forms of systemic risk if liquidity constraints and valuation opacity are not adequately addressed by market participants and regulators.

title: Not Just Extra Chairs in the Classroom: International Student Struggles with Loneliness and Isolation
affiliations: Northeastern University

detail.title: Not Just Extra Chairs in the Classroom: International Student Struggles with Loneliness and Isolation
detail.abstract: International students in a Japanese university struggled with issues of loneliness, lack of belonging, and feelings of not mattering. These issues inhibited their ability to form friendships with domestic students. This study sought to investigate causes and find actionable solutions to international student social networking issues. Participants and data collected in Cycle 1 consisted of international students who offered their experiential insights through ten semi-structured interviews. Alongside domestic and international students, steps were designed, implemented, and evaluated in Cycle 2 in order to empower the international student minority group, and encourage interaction and social bonds between international and domestic students. The Cultural Awareness Circle was founded and met on Mondays throughout the course of the 2023/24 fall semester. 12 meetings were held in which both international and domestic students planned and implemented two mixer events with the goal of increasing international and domestic student interaction and fostering a sense of community. Evaluating the results of the Action Research study included a thorough assessment through member checking, questionnaires, and an exit interview with a participating international student. Student participants and collaborators/allies provided feedback that assisted in the research design and evaluation process. The study concluded that the Cultural Awareness Circle empowered student participants to plan and implement two mixer events that positively impacted international students’ ability to form friendships and interact with their fellow classmates. Implications for the organization included increased intercultural interaction, integration of international student populations, and increased feelings of positivity towards the university by both international and domestic students.

title: Channel Selection with Dynamic Assortment Optimization and Pricing
affiliations: , City University of Hong Kong and University of British Columbia

detail.title: Channel Selection with Dynamic Assortment Optimization and Pricing
detail.abstract: Choice-based revenue management typically assumes a fixed set of sales channels and focuses on dynamically optimizing prices or assortments over a finite horizon. We depart from this paradigm by endogenizing the channel architecture itself. We study a two-stage framework in which a firm first selects its selling channels-subject to cardinality, budget, or matroid constraints-and then dynamically controls assortments and prices under non-replenishable capacity. Within this framework, we formulate three problems: (i) channel selection with dynamic assortment optimization (CwA), (ii) channel selection with dynamic assortment optimization and pricing (CwAP), and (iii) channel-item (edge) selection with dynamic assortment optimization (CIwA), which allows product-level activation across channels. These problems couple a combinatorial design layer with a high-dimensional stochastic dynamic program and lack classical diminishing-returns structure due to endogenous no-purchase effects. To address this challenge, we develop a parametric fluid-based surrogate framework that restores submodularity or γ-cover submodularity through an auxiliary construction. This enables efficient algorithms with provable constant-factor approximation guarantees for the overall stochastic problem across all three settings. On the theoretical side, our analysis yields the first constant-factor approximation guarantee for monotone γ-cover submodular maximization under matroid constraints. On the execution side, we strengthen existing results for dynamic assortment optimization by deriving an improved constant guarantee via refined Bernoulli tail bounds. Together, these results provide a unified approximation framework for integrating combinatorial channel design with dynamic pricing and assortment optimization under capacity constraints.

title: How Artificial Intelligence Shapes Science: Evidence from AlphaFold
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley and Kellogg School of Management

detail.title: How Artificial Intelligence Shapes Science: Evidence from AlphaFold
detail.abstract: We study how a frontier AI model affects scientific discovery by examining the release of the AlphaFold2 algorithm and the impact it had on structural biology and related fields of science. Structural biology is the field of science concerned with understanding the structure and function of proteins, and researchers in this field historically devoted substantial time and resources to experimentally solving three-dimensional protein structures. AlphaFold has the ability to predict these structures without running experiments. In July 2021, researchers gained access to hundreds of thousands of AI-predicted protein structures virtually overnight. Yet, we find that the rate of experimental structure determination remains almost unchanged. Instead, researchers appear to use predicted structures to complement experimental structure determination. Looking at downstream science that builds on protein structures, we find evidence of more basic research occurring on proteins that had no structure information prior to AlphaFold. However, we find no evidence so far that more applied, early-stage drug development is targeting these proteins.

title: Decision Architecture Calibration

detail.title: Decision Architecture Calibration

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests related to this work
declarations.ethicsApproval: Thsi manuscript is conceptual on nature and does not involve human participants, personal data, or experimental procedures. No ethics approval was required
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no funding or grant from any funding agency in public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors

detail.abstract:
Strategic shifts, organisational transformations and digital deployments frequently redistribute decision authority within complex institutions. Yet the redesign of decision rights, escalation pathways and delegation boundaries is often treated as secondary to structural change itself. As a result, formal authority structures persist while execution adapts around them. Under fiscal constraint and digital embedding, informal escalation expands, override becomes habitual and behaviour diverges from design.

This paper introduces Decision Architecture Calibration (DAC) as a disciplined method for designing, stress-testing and periodically realigning decision systems under operational strain, fiscal pressure and technological acceleration. Drawing on organisation design theory, decision-rights frameworks, institutional change scholarship and contemporary AI governance practice, the paper argues that existing approaches address fragments of authority design but do not integrate escalation engineering, delegation staging, workflow embedding and fiscal cadence into a coherent execution discipline.

DAC treats authority not as a static assignment nor as a decaying system, but as an architecture that hardens over time and must be deliberately recalibrated as strategic and environmental conditions shift. It proposes structured articulation of decision rights, interrogation of behaviour under stress, realignment of authority boundaries and institutionalised recalibration at defined junctures such as restructurings, digital deployments and fiscal resets.

By positioning authority design as infrastructural maintenance rather than compliance documentation, Decision Architecture Calibration offers a method for preserving execution stability in environments characterised by institutional pressure and technological acceleration.

title: Institutional and Procedural Aspects of Military Justice
affiliations: Mississippi College - School of Law

detail.title: Institutional and Procedural Aspects of Military Justice
detail.abstract: This is a forthcoming chapter in Litigating International Crimes and Human Rights Violations in U.S. Courts, edited by Mark Klamberg, Milena Sterio, and Douglas Irvin-Erickson. This chapter assesses key features of U.S. military justice, describes the culture of lawyering among U.S. JAG officers, and gives a report card on the suitability of the U.S. military justice system to address core international crimes.

title: Impact Investing and Social Entrepreneurship under Imperfect Monitoring
affiliations: , City University of NY, Baruch College, Zicklin School of Business and Fuqua School of Business, Duke University

detail.title: Impact Investing and Social Entrepreneurship under Imperfect Monitoring
detail.abstract: We develop a theory of impact investing and social entrepreneurship under imperfect monitoring. A socially minded watchdog sets mandated standards in the presence of limited oversight, while a profit-maximizing financier contracts with entrepreneurs who may hold social preferences. When monitoring is effective, regulation binds and socially responsible behavior is cosmetic: equilibrium actions just comply with the mandate regardless of who is financed. When monitoring is weak, the financier hires socially minded entrepreneurs and induces over-compliance, extracting rents from their social preferences. The model characterizes how monitoring efficiency and entrepreneurial values jointly shape equilibrium behavior, entrepreneurial financial returns, the prevalence of impact investing and social entrepreneurship, and welfare. We also discuss empirical implications, paths to empirical engagement, and implications for entrepreneurs, financiers, and institutional design.

detail.abstract:
When leaders demand conformity, employees adapt. They don't stop having views; they stop surfacing them. The result looks like alignment. It rarely is.

This brief examines what conformity-demanding leadership actually produces: managed compliance, emotional exhaustion, diminished voice, and turnover. It draws on research in organizational behavior, facades of conformity, and psychological safety to assess the organizational cost of patterns named in Brief 1, Positional Aggression and Discursive Distancing: A Diagnostic Brief on Observable Leadership Power Patterns and Organizational Impact (Adams-Qualtiere, 2026, https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6133326).

It further argues that this cost is not evenly distributed. The burden falls hardest on those furthest from the organization's unspoken default and that disparity is not a diversity problem. It is a leadership accountability problem.

Addressing these dynamics requires structural leadership discipline that reduces the cost of authenticity, aligns operating values with stated commitments, and and interrupts the adaptive strategies employees have learned to rely on when belonging feels conditional. Written for executive leaders seeking practical clarity rather than academic debate, this brief forms the second installment in a three-part series examining power, cost, and alternative leadership formation.

Key Insight

Employees do not arrive as a blank slate. Leaders inherit individuals whose relationship to authority has already been shaped by prior institutional experiences, including scrutiny, conditional belonging, and expectations tied to who they are rather than what they do. Under these conditions, what leaders may interpret as resistance or disengagement can reflect pattern recognition and adaptive self-protection rather than opposition.

title: Wealth Inequality Reduction as a Climate Change Policy? Evidence on Political Channels

detail.title: Wealth Inequality Reduction as a Climate Change Policy? Evidence on Political Channels
detail.abstract: Economic inequalities potentially affect climate change through two main channels: consumption and policy-making. Existing empirical research primarily identifies a direct, positive relationship between income inequality reduction and CO2 emissions from fossil fuels - largely driven by adverse consumption effects. However, these studies neglect the role of political processes, which introduce temporal lags in decarbonization outcomes. This paper addresses this gap by explicitly accounting for political mechanisms in two novel ways. First, it uses wealth (rather than income) inequality as a proxy for political power. Second, it considers CO2 emissions from land use change (rather than from fossil fuels), as a directly politically-driven and non-temporally delayed environmental outcome. Using a two-stage least squares estimator for a panel of 165 countries from 2000 to 2023, I show that lower wealth inequality decreases land use change emissions. The effect is most pronounced when inequality is measured by the top 10% wealth share and in developing countries, where land use change emissions constitute the majority of total emissions. The findings indicate that inequality reduction and climate change mitigation are not contradictory goals and underscore the importance of integrating political channels into empirical analyses of the inequality-environment nexus.

detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly operate under conditions of acceleration, where signal density, decision tempo, and consequence velocity compress traditional governance cycles. Under such conditions, operational commitment often precedes interpretive comprehension, producing authority lag and oscillatory patterns of expansion and constraint. This paper develops a structural governance architecture — Dual Loops and the Cadence Bridge — designed to preserve directional stability under acceleration. Dual Loops differentiate performance and integrity authority channels, preventing measurable reinforcement from silently redefining institutional intent. The Cadence Bridge introduces event-aligned authority re-entry, replacing static calendar-based review with elastic temporal governance. Cadence Struts operationalize this principle through domain-specific governance channels that flex in response to signal amplitude, volatility, and value at risk while maintaining bounded oversight. Although applicable across analogue, automated, and hybrid environments, adaptive AI systems represent the most compressed stress case of temporal misalignment. By positioning authority distribution and cadence alignment as first-order organization design variables, the framework extends governance theory beyond episodic compliance toward structured stewardship of direction under acceleration.

title: The RRR Selection Mechanism: A Structural Account of Recognition Failure at Senior Professional Levels

detail.title: The RRR Selection Mechanism: A Structural Account of Recognition Failure at Senior Professional Levels

keywords: professional presence Subject classification: Organisational Behaviour

detail.abstract:
This paper identifies a structural friction in senior professional selection that precedes formal evaluation: the Recognition–Evaluation Gap. Standard professional development frameworks operate under the Evaluation Assumption — the premise that career trajectory is a direct function of merit and that selection failure signals deficiency at the performance layer. This paper argues that the Evaluation Assumption mislocates the governing constraint. Before evaluation is possible, a field of consideration must be assembled. That assembly is governed by recognition: a rapid, categorical process operating under bounded rationality that determines whether a professional enters the set of options from which evaluation proceeds.

The paper proposes the RRR Mechanism — a three-gate sequential framework comprising Relatability (accurate placement within an active situational prototype), Relevance (passage of a necessity threshold under loss-aversion-weighted constraint assessment), and Rememberability (retrieval at the moment of decision assembly through associative dominance). The mechanism draws on established foundations in decision science: Simon’s bounded rationality, Rosch’s prototype theory, and the decision science of Kahneman and Tversky — specifically Prospect Theory (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979) and the availability heuristic (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973). The three gates are sequential and non-compensatory. Failure at an upstream gate is not correctable through intervention at a downstream gate.

The paper further develops the dynamics of Compound Gate Failure: the condition in which gate failures interact through feedback loops to produce a self-reinforcing lower-intensity equilibrium — structurally invisible at the surface level of professional activity, and resistant to correction through performance-layer intervention. A multiplicative probability model illustrates how modest alignment deficits at each gate produce disproportionate aggregate contraction of selection probability.

The paper concludes that effective structural recalibration requires diagnostic identification of the gate of primary failure prior to any intervention strategy. The engineering of that recalibration — the diagnostic methodology, intervention sequence, and review discipline — constitutes the applied domain of the broader FutureIsMade research programme and its P3R System.

detail.abstract: Digital government is widely assumed to reduce administrative burdens by replacing bureaucratic encounters with streamlined digital procedures. Yet preliminary evidence from Mexico's ALMP program Jóvenes Construyendo el Futuro suggests a more complex reality. Drawing on a pilot survey measuring digital administrative burdens (n = 123) and preliminary qualitative interviews with program beneficiaries, this paper examines how citizens actually experience enrollment in a digital-by-default public program. While respondents report relatively low learning costs associated with identifying eligibility and program benefits, compliance and psychological costs remain salient, particularly in relation to the time required to complete procedures, uncertainty during the enrollment process, and the need to seek assistance from third parties. Interviews with participants further indicate that access to the program frequently depends on mediation by schools, workplaces, and other actors that help applicants navigate the digital platform. Drawing on the administrative burden framework (Herd & Moynihan, 2018) and sociotechnical perspectives on digital governance (Gil-Garcia et al., 2018; Margetts & Dunleavy, 2013), this paper conceptualizes these dynamics as being part of a broader and culturally-shaped ecosystem of public access. The analysis suggests that in societies like Mexico digitalization reorganizes rather than eliminates bureaucratic friction, producing hybrid arrangements in which digital platforms and social mediation operate simultaneously, undermining (or at the very least profoundly reshaping) the digital-by-default paradigm.

detail.abstract: This study examines the effect of information and communication technology (ICT) usage on labor market outcomes in Palestine, with a focus on real daily wages and hours worked. The study is motivated by the growing importance of digital technologies in shaping productivity, job access, and earnings, especially in developing and conflict-affected economies where physical mobility, market access, and employment opportunities are often severely constrained. While a growing literature documents positive labor-market returns to digital skills and internet access, micro-level evidence for Palestine remains scarce despite the country's pronounced digital divide, persistent labor market fragmentation, and recent destruction of communications infrastructure. Using panel data from the Palestinian Labor Force Survey for the period 2022-2024, this paper constructs a composite ICT usage index and estimates its relationship with labor outcomes using pooled ordinary least squares, individual fixed effects, and an instrumental-variables approach. The results show that ICT usage is positively and significantly associated with wages. In the baseline estimates, a one-unit increase in the ICT usage index is associated with approximately a 9.8 percent increase in daily wages, while the fixed-effects estimate suggests a smaller but still significant within-individual wage gain of about 1 percent. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the wage return to ICT usage is stronger for men than for women and is larger in Gaza and rural areas, suggesting that digital tools may be especially valuable where traditional labor-market access is most constrained.

detail.abstract:
The proliferation of ungoverned processes in financial institutions (Shadow IT) represents a systemic threat to data integrity and regulatory compliance. This paper presents the Secure Low-Code Decision Protocol (SLDP), a technical governance framework that resolves the tension between regulatory control and operational agility in regulated financial environments.

The SLDP extends the Medallion data architecture (Bronze, Silver, Gold) with a proprietary fourth layer called Platinum, combined with Zero Trust security controls, creating an auditable boundary between critical data and the low-code applications that consume it. Governance is embedded in the technical structure, not dependent on user behavior.

Empirical validation was conducted at Banco Santander Brasil (G-SIB) across a R$18 billion (USD 3.6 billion) portfolio. Results: decision latency reduced from 4.5 minutes to real time; 7 parallel Excel systems replaced by a single governed data source across 1,200 users and 21 regional offices; early delinquency reversed from 1.8% to 0.8% within 90 days; 87% of regional units migrated out of critical performance zone; R$208 million (USD 40 million) in loan loss provision savings.

The framework demonstrates direct transferability to U.S. community banks. With USD 1.26 trillion in CRE loan maturities projected for 2027 and community banks carrying average CRE concentrations of 48.2%, the ability to consolidate and act on credit data in minutes, with full regulatory auditability, is a solvency-level concern. The SLDP was built precisely to address this problem.

title: Minimal Stability Geometry of Dimensional Human Physics

detail.title: Minimal Stability Geometry of Dimensional Human Physics
detail.abstract: Dimensional Human Field Theory (DHFT) identifies a closed explanatory architecture. The Dimensional Human Physics (DHP) spine specifies lawful mechanics of load, constraint, accumulation, movement, and time. The present paper provides the first minimal nonlinear dynamical formalization consistent with that spine. A three-variable structural system is specified comprising capacity C(t), boundary permeability B(t), and effective load L(t). Instability is governed by a stability margin κ(C,B) determined by the interaction of structural capacity and boundary integrity. Load accumulation occurs when input exceeds the system's dissipation capacity.

title: Combining Informational and Emotional Advertising Content in Competitive Purchase Funnels
affiliations: CUNY Baruch College, Texas A&M University - Department of Marketing and Texas A&M University

detail.title: Combining Informational and Emotional Advertising Content in Competitive Purchase Funnels
detail.abstract: In practice, firms often combine product information with emotional appeals in their advertising, yet how they should optimally design this advertising content mix in competitive markets remains unclear. We develop a game-theoretic model in which competing firms choose their mix of informational and emotional advertising content to influence consumer search and purchase decisions along a purchase funnel. Advertising content affects competition through two mechanisms: it can draw consumers into the funnel by helping them recognize product fit (a market-converting effect) and steer which firm consumers search first (a search-switching effect). When consumers' prior belief about product fit is low, informational content drives both mechanisms, leading firms to rely exclusively on informational content even when few consumers ultimately find the product a good fit. When prior beliefs are high, however, informational and emotional content drive the two mechanisms separately, creating a strategic tension that leads firms to combine both content types. The implications of this combination depend critically on pricing. Under exogenously fixed pricing, combining content types produces a lose-lose outcome that leaves the market partially uncovered in equilibrium. Under endogenously flexible pricing, by contrast, it becomes a win-win outcome by sustaining higher equilibrium prices for both firms. Firms that rely relatively more on emotional content also offer price discounts more frequently. We further examine how advertising content strategies vary with competitive conditions. As competition intensifies, either through a larger number of competitors or greater overlap in consumer bases, firms increase the share of emotional content. Although weaker firms might be expected to rely more on emotional content to offset their competitive disadvantage, our model shows that this occurs only in niche or highly differentiated markets. In mainstream markets with limited vertical differentiation, the pattern reverses: market followers rely more heavily on informational content than market leaders. Our findings provide a theoretical explanation for the diverse advertising content strategies observed across industries and among close competitors, and offer guidance for managers designing content strategies under different competitive environments.

title: Guardian Angel: A Last-Mile Virtue-Ethics Guardrail for Decentralized Agentic AI Safety

detail.title: Guardian Angel: A Last-Mile Virtue-Ethics Guardrail for Decentralized Agentic AI Safety

publicationDetails.detailsText: Stanford University Graduate School of Business Research Paper No. undefined

detail.abstract: Agentic AI systems introduce novel safety challenges that upstream alignment layers cannot fully address. Prompt injection, emotional manipulation, and infrastructure-disabling actions can bypass model-level safeguards, leading to unauthorized tool executions with real-world consequences. We present Guardian Angel, a deployable plugin for open agent frameworks (e.g., OpenClaw/ClawHub) that enforces moral oversight at the last mile-immediately before tool calls-via a privileged before_tool_call hook. Grounded in Thomistic virtue ethics and centered on caritas (the willing of the principal's genuine good), the system maintains a continuous virtuous disposition while applying triggered three-gate evaluation: provenance classification, intrinsic-evil hard stops, and virtue-based scoring using a Clarity × Stakes matrix. Questionable actions escalate to human approval via cryptographically bound, time-limited nonces. The design exploits a key structural property of agentic systems-the sparsity of tool calls relative to internal reasoning-to integrate fast System 1 filtering with deliberate System 2 moral reasoning, thereby decentralizing safety to end-users without prohibitive latency. We discuss the philosophical prerequisites for such systems, detail the architecture and implementation, present qualitative evaluation results from red-team testing, and outline directions for formal benchmarking. Guardian Angel is MIT-0 licensed and available at https://clawhub.ai/leo3linbeck/guardian-angel.

detail.abstract: South Africa entered the COVID-19 pandemic with one of the world's most unequal labor markets, where racial stratification shaped not only employment access but the distribution of wages within employment. This paper estimates the differential effect of the post-2020 period on monthly wages using seven waves of the Labor Market Dynamics in South Africa (LMDSA) dataset spanning 2017 to 2023. The empirical strategy employs a difference-indifferences design with race-by-post-2020 interaction terms, conditional on province, year-by-quarter, education, industry, and occupation fixed effects, with standard errors clustered at the survey stratum level. The results show that racial wage inequality widened sharply and persistently after 2020 across all subgroups examined. Among wage employees, African/Black workers experienced a relative wage penalty of approximately 37 percent and Colored workers approximately 52 percent. The most striking finding concerns employers: African/Black business owners suffered a relative earnings loss of approximately 59 percent, entirely reversing a modest pre-pandemic advantage, exposing the fragility of post-apartheid entrepreneurial gains. Gender-disaggregated estimates reveal larger conditional penalties for non-White men than women among the employed, though this coexists with documented severe labor force exclusion of women during the crisis. Occupational strata analysis confirms that penalties are present across all skill levels and are not explained by compositional sorting across industries or occupations. These findings are consistent with a structural amplifier interpretation, whereby the pandemic revealed and entrenched pre-existing vulnerabilities in a segmented labor market rather than generating new ones.

detail.abstract:
This Supreme Court amicus brief--filed by the Georgetown Law Appellate Courts Immersion Clinic--concerns whether a federal law deregulating the commercial-trucking industry preempts state-law suits against commercial truck brokers whose negligence causes costly, and often deadly, truck crashes. The brief was filed on behalf of the Institute for Safer Trucking, a non-profit organization that supports survivors of truck crashes and families of victims. The Institute aims to reduce truck crashes, injuries, and fatalities by educating the public, the trucking industry, and lawmakers about data-driven solutions such as minimum-insurance increases for interstate motor carriers and the adoption of safety technologies.

In the commercial-trucking industry, freight brokers serve as intermediaries. Brokers handle logistics for shippers (who want their goods distributed around the country) by hiring motor carriers (who operate commercial trucks) to transport the shippers’ goods.

The brief explains why Congress did not preempt suits against brokers whose negligence causes calamitous truck crashes. Part I of the brief shows how carriers and brokers operate, how federal law does (and does not) regulate them, and how they work together to move goods around the country. This part explains that brokers are often the only parties with the financial resources to provide adequate remedies when their negligent hiring practices lead to crashes. Part II provides examples of crashes in which brokers’ negligence left motorists dead or catastrophically injured. Finally, Part III explains why, under governing federal-preemption doctrine, it makes no sense to immunize brokers from state common-law liability.

Notably,  law students in Georgetown Law’s Appellate Courts Immersion Clinic -- Max Rosenthal, Zarah Zhao, Nicky Downs, and Sean LaLiberte -- made major contributions to this brief.

title: Categories and Social Evaluations
affiliations: and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: Categories and Social Evaluations
detail.abstract: One of the developments over the past twenty years in strategy and organisations research is the general recognition that participants in organisational fields such as industries and markets make sense of field conditions, events, and themselves partially through collective cognitive representations that summarise important similarities and differences among field actors and objects and parse them into subjective categories. Categorical representations both include (category members) and exclude (category non-members) and, thus, represent the basic identity distinctions that underpin organisational fields. Our chapter in this Oxford Handbook maps the relationship between such representations and the structure and dynamics of social evaluations within organisational fields. Our goals are threefold. First, we provide a brief review of the major research studies and themes on organisational categories that have emerged in the literature to inform our understanding of how such categories develop and function. Second, we examine research on this influence, and we organise and systematise the consequences of category inclusion, exclusion, and spillovers. Third, we advance an agentic perspective to characterise how actors in fields are not passive category takers who simply accept the categorical memberships that others place upon them-they are also category makers who, if savvy enough, can strategically shape the categorical interpretations used by others to interpret their actions and characteristics. Ultimately, this underscores how categories are co-constructed by a variety of actors within a field, and it emphasises possibilities for strategic action. We conclude our chapter by discussing possible lines of future research that we believe are especially promising.

title: Are We Ready? From Vocabulary Switch to Regime Switch in Disclosure Demand
affiliations: Saint Mary's University, Canada

detail.title: Are We Ready? From Vocabulary Switch to Regime Switch in Disclosure Demand
detail.abstract: Public debate surrounding unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) frequently centers on a practical policy demand: disclosure. While some observers actively advocate for immediate disclosure, a substantial share of the population currently devotes little attention to the issue. This paper examines how shifts in public attention may influence the evolution of disclosure demand. The analysis considers a population composed of attentive agents who support disclosure and cannot-care-right-now (CCRN) agents who remain largely inattentive. Government communications-including hearings, reports, and related signals-may shift individuals from the CCRN group into the attentive population. The model predicts that when attention activation interacts with social influence, the system may transition rapidly toward a common consensus supporting disclosure once a sufficient share of previously inattentive individuals becomes attentive. The paper therefore examines whether institutions are prepared for the possibility that increased public attention could trigger very rapid convergence of public opinion toward a disclosure demand.

title: From Knowledge to Purpose: The Shifting Bottleneck of Value Creation and Five Domains of Human Value as We Approach AGI

detail.title: From Knowledge to Purpose: The Shifting Bottleneck of Value Creation and Five Domains of Human Value as We Approach AGI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Founder and CEO of Dixon AI Ltd, an AI consultancy and training provider. The frameworks discussed in this paper, including the PEJ framework and the AI Capability framework, inform the consultancy's commercial offerings. The author is also a Lecturer at Manchester Metropolitan University. No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
The question dominating public debate, 'Will AI take my job?', is the wrong question. The right question is: what happens to human economic value when intelligence becomes cheap? This paper argues that economic history is a story of shifting bottlenecks. In agrarian economies, the constraint was land and labour. In industrial economies, it was capital and machinery. In the knowledge economy, the bottleneck is human intelligence: the ability to analyse, synthesise, advise, and decide. Generative AI changes that. When machines can perform large portions of knowledge work at near-zero marginal cost, intelligence ceases to be the scarce resource. The bottleneck shifts again, this time to purpose: deciding what is worth doing, why it matters, and whether the outcomes are acceptable.

Drawing on the Purpose, Execution, Judgement (PEJ) framework and the AI Capability model established in a companion paper (Dixon, 2026b), this paper decomposes the transition from a knowledge-based to a purpose-based economy. Historically, knowledge workers bundled Purpose, Execution, and Judgement together. AI breaks that bundle apart. Execution becomes increasingly automated. Purpose and Judgement remain human domains, not because machines are incapable of approximating them, but because ceding them would represent an irreversible transfer of agency from human to machine (Dixon, 2025d).

The paper identifies five enduring domains of human economic value in the emerging purpose-based economy: purpose-setting, judgement and accountability, empathy, authenticity, and continuous learning. A distinctive contribution is the argument that empathy and authenticity possess intrinsic economic value derived not from functional capability but from human choice itself: the knowledge that another human being chose to care, or chose to create. This engages with and extends care ethics and the philosophy of authenticity. The paper advances six formal propositions, offers a shifting bottleneck model of economic transitions, and discusses implications for leaders, educators, and policymakers navigating the most consequential economic transition of the twenty-first century.

detail.abstract: The proliferation of low-cost unmanned aerial systems (UAS) has created an unprecedented cost-exchange asymmetry in modern air defense, exemplified by the expenditure of $3-5 million interceptor missiles against drone threats costing as little as $20,000. This quantitative study conducted a comprehensive cost-effectiveness analysis of counter-UAS (C-UAS) technologies across kinetic, electronic warfare (EW), and directed energy weapon (DEW) domains during the critical period of 2022-2026. Utilizing publicly available datasets from Oryx, SIPRI, and ACLED, combined with defense industry specifications and operational data from the Ukraine conflict, this research developed and applied the Multi-Layered Defense Economics Model (MLDEM) to evaluate 19 distinct C-UAS systems against standardized threat profiles. The analysis employed descriptive statistics, Kruskal-Wallis H-tests, Mann-Whitney U-tests, multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA), and Monte Carlo simulation with 10,000 iterations to assess cost-effectiveness metrics, technology readiness, and operational sustainability. Results revealed that cost-per-engagement (CPE) varies by more than five orders of magnitude across system categories, ranging from approximately $0.01 for EW systems to $4.75 million for advanced missile interceptors. Statistical analysis demonstrated significant differences between technology categories (H = 13.92, p = 0.0009, ε² = 0.745), with DEW and gun-based kinetic systems achieving consistently favorable cost-exchange ratios against mass drone threats. Hypotheses H1a, H1b, and H2 were supported, indicating that DEW systems achieve CPE ratios below $500 per engagement, gun-based systems below $2,000 per engagement, and multi-layered architectures outperform single-technology solutions. Hypothesis H3, positing a positive correlation between technology readiness level and cost-effectiveness, was not supported (ρ = -0.404, p = 0.086). These findings provide empirical foundations for defense acquisition decisions, demonstrating that economically sustainable C-UAS architectures require a diversified technology portfolio prioritizing directed energy and gun-based effectors over missile systems for high-volume drone defense scenarios.
